tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer
tools.description:
Use a mouse and keyboard to interact with a web browser, and take screenshots. If you don't have a valid tab ID, use tabs_context_mcp first to get available tabs.
* Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element before moving the cursor.
* If you tried clicking on a program or link but it failed to load, even after waiting, try adjusting your click location so that the tip of the cursor visually falls on the element that you want to click.
* Make sure to click any buttons, links, icons, etc with the cursor tip in the center of the element. Don't click boxes on their edges unless asked.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported and will return an error - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels. Requires a Claude in Chrome extension version that supports scale; older extensions return the full-size image.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tabId.description: Tab ID to execute the action on. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

save_to_disk.description: For screenshot/zoom actions: save the image to disk so it can be attached to a message for the user. Returns the saved path in the tool result. Only set this when you intend to share the image — screenshots you're just looking at don't need saving.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate
tools.description: Navigate to a URL, or go forward/back in browser history. tabId may be omitted for URL navigation when calling navigate STANDALONE (not inside browser_batch): tabs_context_mcp{createIfEmpty:true} is called for you and the first tab in the session's group is navigated — its result is appended to this call's output so you have the tab list and ids for subsequent calls. tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page
tools.description: Get an accessibility tree representation of elements on the page. By default returns all elements including non-visible ones. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default. If the output exceeds this limit it is truncated at a line boundary, with a note giving the full size — pass a larger max_chars, or use depth/ref_id to focus on part of the page. filter.description: Filter elements: "interactive" for buttons/links/inputs only, "all" for all elements including non-visible ones (default: all elements)

tabId.description: Tab ID to read from. Must be a tab in the current group. Use tabs_context_mcp first if you don't have a valid tab ID.

depth.description: Maximum depth of the tree to traverse (default: 15). Use a smaller depth if output is too large.

ref_id.description: Reference ID of a parent element to read. Will return the specified element and all its children. Use this to focus on a specific part of the page when output is too large.

max_chars.description: Maximum characters for output (default: 50000). Set to a higher value if your client can handle large outputs.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp
tools.description: Close a tab in the MCP tab group by its ID. Use to clean up tabs you're done with. Only tabs in this session's group are closable; call tabs_context_mcp first to get valid IDs. If you close the group's last tab, Chrome auto-removes the group — the next tabs_context_mcp with createIfEmpty starts fresh.

tabId.description: The ID of the tab to close. Must be in this session's tab group. Get valid IDs from tabs_context_mcp.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp
tools.description: Get context information about the current MCP tab group. Returns all tab IDs inside the group if it exists. CRITICAL: You must get the context at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Each new conversation should create its own new tab (using tabs_create_mcp) rather than reusing existing tabs, unless the user explicitly asks to use an existing tab.

createIfEmpty.description: Creates a new MCP tab group if none exists, creates a new Window with a new tab group containing an empty tab (which can be used for this conversation). If a MCP tab group already exists, this parameter has no effect.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
tools.description: Creates a new empty tab in the MCP tab group. CRITICAL: You must get the context using tabs_context_mcp at least once before using other browser automation tools so you know what tabs exist. Tabs you create are yours to clean up: close each one with tabs_close_mcp as soon as you no longer need it, and close any that remain before finishing your task. Leave a tab open only if the user asked to see it or wants it kept open.

content.text: Meta AI has replied. Reading its review:

Title: Meta AI - Your AI Assistant for Images, Shopping and More
URL: https://www.meta.ai/prompt/37905ade-5f45-4dbe-83ba-c4b1faeda481
Source element: <main>
---
Reviewing Loka provenance paper
loka-retractable-provenance
PDF
You are a critical peer reviewer for a systems/databases venue. Review the attached paper, which is about to be submitted to arXiv (cs.DB). Give: (1) a one-paragraph summary; (2) a recommendation (Strong Accept / Accept / Weak Accept / Weak Reject / Reject); (3) the main weaknesses, each with the section it concerns and a concrete fix; (4) any claims that are overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent with the paper's own tables; (5) minor issues (clarity, terminology, citations). Be specific and cite section numbers.
Today
Show thinking

This is a careful, unusually honest systems paper. Here is a peer review for arXiv cs.DB before submission:

(1) Summary

Loka is an RDF-star triplestore that stores model-predicted triples alongside curated Wikidata triples, with each generated triple carrying a fixed RDF-star annotation block in a reserved namespace http://loka.dev/provenance/: propositionGenerated, propositionGeneratedBy, propositionConfidence, propositionSelectedFrom (quoted triples), etc. The namespace is excluded from training corpora via a SPARQL-star FILTER NOT EXISTS (§3.1), and the same edges are used for cascade retraction: deleting a node removes its triples and, transitively, any generated triple whose propositionSelectedFrom points at a removed triple (§3.4). Retraction is node-rooted, follows only reserved-namespace edges, and is exposed as preview + confirmed delete. The case study trains a series of small role-aware transformers v3-v14 from scratch on label-substituted Wikidata (up to 4M triples), with a bounded candidate selector that proposes (s,p) slots from neighbourhood overlap and writes at most 40 citations per prediction (§4.4). Evaluation tests retraction correctness against an independent reference on synthetic graphs (700 roots), times retraction on 5k-5M row stores, compares against a SPARQL-star closure baseline (6-10x slower), and runs on two real Wikidata stores (153k and 2M triples) with 2-hop chains, checking 4,354 and 8,621 required removals respectively. Encoding cost vs reification and named graphs is measured, and link-prediction accuracy is reported as below a predicate-frequency baseline (§6.4).

(2) Recommendation

Weak Accept for arXiv, with mandatory fixes. For a top-tier systems/DB venue: Weak Reject in current form – the provenance machinery is sound and well-artifacted (code, checkpoints, corpora released, retraction bug found and fixed via reference test §6.1), but evaluation is single-machine, single-threaded, limited to 2-hop chains, and the core provenance claim is procedurally complete but semantically weak by design. The paper should be published after addressing §3.1, §3.4/§7.2 and §6.2 issues below.

(3) Main weaknesses

W1 – Store-level guarantee is hollow (§3.1). You claim three-layer exclusion keeps generated triples out of corpora and system metadata out of model I/O. The last paragraph of §3.1 admits: "All of these guards sit in Loka's extractor and inference pipeline, not in the store:... the store accepts any triple over POST /triples, so a generated triple that another tool writes without the generated flag is not excluded." This contradicts §3.1 bullet 1 and Abstract. Fix: move prefix + flag filter into the storage engine's write path, or restate the guarantee as pipeline-only and add a store-side validator. Document what a non-Loka writer must do.

W2 – Retraction semantics over-deletes and leaves orphans (§3.4, §7.2). Two admitted limitations break correctness: (a) "One justification per triple" – if two writers store identical triple with different citation sets, citation sets merge and retracting source of either removes the triple (§7.2). This violates monotonic counting of alternative derivations (Gupta et al. 1993, §2.5). (b) "Curated annotations outlive their triple" – retracting a curated statement leaves its Wikidata qualifiers/references as annotations on an unasserted quoted triple, so store remains well-formed per RDF-star but describes a statement it no longer holds. Fix: (a) store citations per derivation, not per triple, with a reference count; retract only when count reaches zero. Or explicitly scope paper to single-writer and enforce uniqueness at write time. (b) sweep non-reserved annotations on removed triples, or flag orphaned quoted triples as tombstones and make extraction filter drop them. Your note that this "would change removal totals" in §6.2 is exactly why it must be fixed – current timings exclude work a correct implementation must do.

W3 – Retraction cost claim rests on two data points (§6.2). You state time follows removal size, not store size. Table 1 shows: 5,034 rows / 1,439 removed -> 0.45 ms, 50k/7,367 -> 2.84 ms, 504k/120k -> 86.3 ms, 5M/106k -> 85.0 ms. Only the last two isolate store size, with overlapping ranges 82-104.6 ms vs 80.5-86.2 ms. You also note absolute times vary 1.6x between sessions within same laptop. Ratio to SPARQL-star is measured in same process, which is good, but both are in-memory index only; persistent sled commit is measured separately with 30 samples and shows 140 ms median before single-transaction fix. Fix: (i) add 95th percentile / variance across sessions, not just across 5 back-to-back runs; (ii) add a second pair isolating store size at smaller removal size; (iii) report persistent store preview vs commit separately and include concurrency (readers during retraction). Do not claim store-size independence from n=2.

W4 – Bounded selector makes provenance incomplete by construction (§4.4, §7.2). Selector consults at most 20 of subject's statements and 20 neighbours, citing everything it used, max 40. Unbounded version cites median 105 (§4.4). Provenance is "complete relative to what the bounded selector consulted" (§7.2) – i.e., a statement beyond first 20 that actually caused a proposal is neither consulted nor cited, so retraction of it will not reach prediction. Fix: log the truncation, store a propositionSelectorTruncated flag, and evaluate recall of required removals under unbounded vs bounded on real graph; §6.5 replaces generator but keeps same bound, so does not test this.

W5 – Link prediction evaluation conflates design choices (§6.4). Entities identified by English label, so distinct entities with same label merge – affects both transformer and TransE equally but inflates predicate-frequency baseline (§7.3). Candidates are objects seen with p in training – same signal frequency baseline uses. No validation split, no tuning for either model, dimension 128 TransE, 20 epochs. MRR 0.129 vs 0.115 is presented as "does not beat baseline" which is correct, but then v13 Hits@1 0.020 vs 0.018 on literal-valued is called "within noise" while being bolded in table. Fix: freeze candidate set independent of baseline (e.g., all entities in corpus), report label-collision rate, and add a simple tuned baseline (RotatE or ComplEx) or explicitly state no method comparison intended. Remove bolding that suggests wins.

(4) Overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent claims

Abstract / §9: "106k-triple removal from a 5M-row store in about 0.1 s". Table §6.2 first table: 5,050,435 rows, 106,255 removed, median 85.0 ms (range 80.5-86.2 ms) – 0.085 s, not 0.1 s, and second table same workload is 71.3 ms (70.2-95.1 ms). Use median-of-medians with session variation disclaimer. Conclusion says "about 0.1 s" – okay rounded, but must cite variation.

§6.2: "matched an independent closure on all 8,621 required removals" (Abstract) / "nothing missed and nothing extra". True for generated triples + reserved annotations only. You explicitly exclude curated annotations that outlive triple (§7.2). The independent closure in §6.2 is defined as "a generated triple must be removed if..." – it does not check curated annotation rows, so agreement does not prove full store consistency. Clarify scope.

§6.3: "RDF-star block is 2.8x smaller than reification". Rows: 333 vs 937 is 2.81x – correct. Bytes: 82,839 vs 125,570 is 1.51x. You are a critical peer reviewer for a systems/databases venue. Review the attached paper, which is about to be submitted to arXiv (cs.DB). Give: (1) a one-paragraph summary; (2) a recommendation (Strong Accept / Accept / Weak Accept / Weak Reject / Reject); (3) the main weaknesses, each with the section it concerns and a concrete fix; (4) any claims that are overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent with the paper's own tables; (5) minor issues (clarity, terminology, citations). Be specific and cite section numbers.

Gemini said

Here is a critical peer review of the submission.

1. One-Paragraph Summary

The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star triplestore and integration architecture designed to track, isolate, and retract model-generated triples alongside curated knowledge graph data. By storing system metadata in a reserved namespace ([http://loka.dev/provenance/](http://loka.dev/provenance/)) via RDF-star quoted triples—specifically recording the generating model, decoding confidence, and "selection provenance" pointers to the stored statements used to propose the candidate slot—the system implements a multi-layer guard ensuring generated statements do not re-enter training corpora. Furthermore, Loka leverages these quoted dependency edges to perform cascade retraction, where removing a root entity automatically sweeps transitively derived generated triples without traversing standard data edges. The authors evaluate retraction correctness and performance against synthetic graphs and sampled Wikidata stores, showing sub-millisecond to sub-second closure computations, while openly documenting the weak generation performance of their internal Transformer baseline.
PDF
+ 4

2. Recommendation

Weak Accept (Leaning Accept for arXiv / Systems Workshop; borderline for top-tier DB conference without addressing architectural baselines).

The paper is remarkably honest about negative results (e.g., the Transformer failing to beat a predicate-frequency baseline) and documents an end-to-end open-source prototype with released artifacts. The core conceptual contribution—using RDF-star quoted triples natively for bounded cascade retraction and corpus-hygiene enforcement—is practical, well-engineered, and timely given the rush to dump LLM-extracted assertions into enterprise knowledge graphs. However, the database contributions are limited in novelty (essentially a specialized transitive closure over an in-memory index vs. plain SPARQL property paths), the storage evaluation lacks comparison against dedicated provenance engines, and several semantic trade-offs (e.g., leaving orphaned curated qualifiers, all-or-nothing node-level retraction) require formalization.
PDF
+ 4

3. Main Weaknesses and Concrete Fixes

Weakness 1: Semantic Asymmetry and Orphaned Curated Annotations during Retraction

Section: §3.4 and §7.2

Issue: The authors note that when a curated triple is removed at depth 0, its reserved-namespace annotations are swept, but curated annotations (e.g., Wikidata qualifiers and references) remain behind on a quoted triple that is no longer asserted. While structurally valid in RDF-star, leaving dangling unasserted provenance/qualifiers is a form of metadata leakage/garbage accumulation that undermines store consistency.
PDF
+ 2

Concrete Fix: Provide a configuration flag or garbage collection pass for retract_set that optionally cascades to unasserted metadata referencing deleted assertion IDs. At minimum, quantify the extent of these dangling qualifier triples in §6.2 when reporting the real-data Wikidata retractions.

Weakness 2: Overly Coarse Node-Level Retraction vs. Statement-Level Retraction

Section: §3.4, §4.4, §7.2

Issue: The engine restricts retraction roots to whole nodes (retract_set) rather than single statements because the candidate selector cites only one statement per contributing neighbor. If a single erroneous fact is corrected on a node (the most common operational scenario in KG curation), Loka cannot surgically retract only the downstream triples derived from that specific fact without deleting the entire entity or suffering false negatives.
PDF
+ 4

Concrete Fix: Clarify why the candidate selector cannot cite all matching statements when bounded to 20 neighbors. If each neighbor contributes at most one predicate match, citing the exact matching statement set for statement-level dependency would add minimal overhead while enabling precise, statement-level truth maintenance.
PDF

Weakness 3: Thin Systems / Triplestore Baselines

Section: §6.2, §6.3

Issue: The retraction performance is only benchmarked against an in-memory index in Loka itself and compared against SPARQL-star queries executed by Loka's own query executor. There is no comparison against external production-grade RDF-star stores (e.g., GraphDB, Jena, or Stardog) evaluating whether standard SPARQL property paths on established engines face the same 6–10× slowdown. Similarly, §6.3 evaluates RDF-star vs. Reification on Loka only, omitting comparison with systems optimized for lineage (like TripleProv).
PDF
+ 3

Concrete Fix: Run the SPARQL-star recursive query benchmark (§6.2) on at least one mature open-source triplestore (e.g., Apache Jena TDB2 with RDF-star support) to validate whether Loka’s dedicated C++/Rust traversal provides an engine-independent benefit over general-purpose query optimizers.

Weakness 4: Single-Derivation Assumption and Over-Deletion

Section: §2.5, §7.2

Issue: The authors assume each generated triple has only one justification and explicitly avoid derivation counting. If another pipeline produces the same triple via a different derivation path, Loka unions the provenance; retracting one path purges the triple entirely.
PDF
+ 2

Concrete Fix: Discuss the computational trade-offs of maintaining a reference counter or multiple discrete provenance graph nodes. In §3.2/§7.2, formalize the condition under which Loka's semantics correspond to a specific provenance semiring (e.g., Boolean/Trio semiring where deletion is pessimistic).

4. Overstated, Unsupported, or Inconsistent Claims

Inconsistency in Benchmark Timings (§6.2, Tables 1 and 2):

In the first table of §6.2, retract_set median times are listed as 0.45 ms (1k), 2.84 ms (10k), 86.3 ms (100k), and 85.0 ms (1M).
PDF

In the baseline comparison table immediately following, retract_set is listed as 0.37 ms (1k), 2.36 ms (10k), 71.5 ms (100k), and 71.3 ms (1M).
PDF

While the text mentions a 15–20% run-to-run variation between distinct binaries, presenting two separate tables side-by-side with differing numbers for the identical operation without unified presentation creates confusion. The authors should merge these or present relative speedups within a single controlled table.
PDF

Unsubstantiated Store-Size Invariance Claim (§6.2, §9):

The conclusion states: "timed at about 0.1 s for a 106k-triple retraction in a 5M-row store, with cost that, on the two large synthetic data points that isolate store size, follows the size of the removal rather than of the store".
PDF

Having only two data points (100k vs 1M generated triples with ~120k and ~106k removed triples) is insufficient to empirically prove asymptotic independence from total store size. This should be phrased as an initial observation consistent with index lookups rather than a demonstrated generalized property.
PDF

Typo in Table Column in §6.5:

In the table of §6.5, the entry for Predicate Frequency citations per prediction reads: 9 / 10.3 19 / / 36. This is a typesetting/formatting error (double slashes and space misplaced in 10.3 / 19 / 36).
PDF

5. Minor Issues (Clarity, Terminology, Citations)

Historical Naming Discrepancy (§3.1):

In §3.1, the authors disclose that propositionSelectedFrom was previously called propositionInferredFrom and that "the engine's retraction still follows the old IRI" for the evaluated stores. State explicitly whether release v0.4.7 aliases both IRIs or standardizes on propositionSelectedFrom for clean reproducibility.
PDF
+ 1

Entity Resolution Ambiguity (§4.4, Step 4):

Step 4 describes mapping labels back to entities if the label "equals the label of exactly one entity in the store". How are homonyms/polysemy handled in the broader Wikidata dump? If an entity label is identical to a common dictionary term or another entity, it defaults to literal, which explains why only 5/356 and 8/672 resolved. This trade-off should be explicitly highlighted in §4.4.
PDF
+ 3

Missing Details on Import Drops (§6.2):

§6.2 notes that on the Q42 neighborhood, "the importer rejected 2,139 lines, 1.4%, and since the pulled file was not kept their cause can no longer be determined". For a systems paper, discarding data without logging error types (e.g., malformed literals, unsupported datatypes, unescaped characters) appears unrigorous; briefly clarify typical parser reject causes in Loka.

Critical peer review: Loka — Provenance for Retracting Model-Generated Triples in an RDF-star Store
Weak Accept

Recommendation for a systems/database venue

1. Summary

The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that records provenance for model-generated triples and uses that provenance to support exclusion from subsequent training corpora and cascading retraction. Its central contribution is a reserved RDF-star annotation schema recording the generating model, confidence score, and selection provenance: the stored statements that caused the inference procedure to propose a particular subject–predicate pair. The system uses these explicit dependency edges to retract generated statements transitively when a source entity is removed, while avoiding traversal through ordinary data relationships. The implementation is evaluated using synthetic dependency graphs and real Wikidata-derived stores, including a 5-million-row synthetic benchmark, a 2-million-triple real-data experiment, and comparisons against SPARQL-star closure queries and alternative RDF provenance encodings. The paper also evaluates its model-generation component against predicate-frequency and TransE baselines, finding that its transformer does not outperform predicate frequency. Importantly, the authors explicitly distinguish procedural provenance from semantic justification: the recorded statements explain why a candidate was proposed, not why the predicted object is correct. Overall, this is a useful systems-engineering contribution with a clearly scoped problem, a concrete implementation, and unusually candid reporting of limitations. Its principal weakness is that the correctness and performance evidence establishes the behavior of one particular bounded selection procedure rather than a general provenance solution for model-generated knowledge graphs.

2. Recommendation
Weak Accept

I would lean toward acceptance as a systems implementation paper, although the contribution is relatively incremental in its underlying algorithms.

Reasons to accept:

The problem is real and clearly motivated: generated knowledge graph statements need to be distinguishable, excluded from training, and retractable when their sources are withdrawn.

The RDF-star representation is straightforward and reasonably elegant. It avoids requiring a separate provenance database or an additional reification layer.

The implementation goes beyond a conceptual schema. It integrates extraction, candidate selection, annotation, inference, and deletion.

The evaluation includes independent reference implementations, actual stores, a SPARQL baseline, and persistent deletion measurements.

The paper is unusually transparent about failure cases, including a correctness defect discovered during evaluation and the fact that the model performs worse than a simple baseline.

Reasons against a stronger recommendation:

The fundamental cascade-retraction algorithm is a specialized dependency-closure traversal, not a substantially new database algorithm.

The provenance semantics are narrower than the terminology might initially suggest.

The evaluation is concentrated on one implementation, one dataset family, and relatively shallow real dependency chains.

The paper does not adequately establish the generality of its performance claims or the completeness of its provenance guarantees outside its particular inference pipeline.

I would not recommend Reject because the paper does deliver a working system and meaningful experimental evidence. However, I would not recommend Accept without qualification because several aspects of the contribution need sharper technical framing.

3. Main weaknesses and concrete fixes
W1. The provenance semantics do not capture the model's actual data dependencies

Major conceptual issue Sections 2.4, 2.6, 3.2, 4.4, 7.2

This is the most important issue in the paper.

The authors carefully distinguish selection provenance from semantic support, which is good. However, there is a deeper distinction that needs to be made explicit: the statements used by the candidate selector are not necessarily the complete set of data dependencies of the generated prediction.

The model is trained on a corpus containing potentially millions of triples. Its parameters can encode information from any of those training examples. At inference time, the model receives only subject and predicate labels, but that does not mean its prediction is independent of the rest of the training corpus.

For example:

A curated Wikidata statement about an entity enters the training corpus.

The transformer learns a statistical association from that statement.

A later prediction uses a candidate selected through an entirely different set of statements.

The selected statements are recorded as provenance.

The original training statement is deleted, but the model's parameters still encode whatever it learned from it.

The retraction procedure will not identify this dependency.

This matters because §2.4 describes cascade retraction as removing a source's influence from model-generated stored outputs, while §2.6 motivates training from scratch on a known corpus partly on the grounds that it keeps the model's learned information within a known dataset.

Those are not equivalent guarantees.

The paper's actual mechanism tracks dependencies of the inference procedure, not dependencies of the model's learned parameters.

Concrete fix:

Explicitly distinguish training-data provenance, candidate-selection provenance, and inference-time input provenance.

State that Loka implements the second category, with a record of the third category's selector inputs.

Clarify that deleting a training example does not remove its influence from an already-trained model.

Narrow the claims in §§2.4 and 2.6 accordingly.

Consider an experiment demonstrating that deleting a source statement does not necessarily eliminate predictions influenced by the model's training on that statement.

I do not consider this a fatal flaw if the contribution is framed as procedural provenance. However, the distinction is central enough that it should be prominent in the abstract and introduction, not merely implicit in the technical discussion.

W2. The retraction guarantees depend on node-level deletion and a bounded selector

Sections 3.4, 4.4, 7.2

The retraction algorithm is presented clearly, but its guarantees are substantially narrower than a general dependency-provenance system.

The selector examines at most 20 subject statements and 20 distinct neighbours. It then records at most one statement per contributing neighbour.

This produces a maximum of 40 citations per prediction, which is a reasonable engineering decision.

However, the resulting completeness guarantee is conditional on the selector's bounded execution and the node-level deletion semantics.

There are two related problems:

First: statement-level deletion.

The paper correctly acknowledges that only one statement per neighbour is recorded. If a different statement belonging to that neighbour is deleted individually, the prediction may remain even though the deleted statement participated in the selection process.

Second: alternative derivations.

If two independent generation procedures produce the same triple, their citation sets merge. The implementation retracts the triple when any cited source disappears.

This is not equivalent to maintaining multiple justifications. A triple with two independent derivations can be deleted even though one derivation remains valid.

The authors acknowledge both limitations in §7.2, but they have implications for the generality of the claimed provenance mechanism.

Concrete fix:

Add a small formal definition of the supported semantics:

Retraction is node-rooted.

Dependencies are OR-style: any cited source disappearing invalidates the generated triple.

There is one merged provenance set per generated triple.

The selector's bounded execution defines the universe of recorded dependencies.

Then distinguish this from statement-level deletion and alternative-derivation-aware truth maintenance.

A particularly useful experiment would compare bounded and unbounded selection on the same dataset, measuring not only annotation volume but also the difference in retraction results.

The paper already reports citation counts of median 9 versus 105 in §4.4. It should also report what additional dependency coverage is lost through bounding, if that can be measured.

W3. The training exclusion guarantee is a pipeline property, not a store invariant

Sections 3.1, 3.3, 5.5

The paper repeatedly emphasizes that generated statements cannot re-enter the training corpus.

The implementation has a sensible three-layer design:

The extractor excludes triples marked as generated.

The selector excludes reserved predicates.

The writer refuses reserved predicates.

However, §3.1 explicitly acknowledges that the store accepts arbitrary triples through its HTTP write interface. An external writer can insert a generated statement without the generated flag.

Such a statement can enter a subsequent training corpus.

Consequently, the system does not enforce a general invariant that generated statements cannot enter training. It enforces an invariant for statements correctly annotated by the Loka inference pipeline.

There is also an asymmetry: excluding generated statements depends on the generated flag, whereas excluding system metadata depends on the reserved namespace.

Concrete fix:

State explicitly that the guarantee applies to outputs written through the instrumented pipeline.

Consider an integration test that inserts an unflagged generated triple and demonstrates the current behavior.

If the intended guarantee is stronger, introduce a store-level write policy or require an explicit provenance classification for externally generated statements.

The current design is defensible, but the distinction between pipeline enforcement and store enforcement should be made unmistakable.

W4. The evaluation does not establish general scalability of the retraction algorithm

Sections 6.1–6.2

The performance evaluation is one of the stronger parts of the paper, but it is not sufficient to support broad scalability claims.

The synthetic benchmark is useful:

The large-store comparison is encouraging: approximately the same removal workload takes approximately the same time in stores differing by an order of magnitude.

However:

The largest retraction set is selected from a sample of 50 roots.

There are only two large-store observations supporting the claim that runtime depends primarily on removal-set size.

The synthetic dependency generator does not establish that real-world provenance graphs have comparable degree distributions.

Real-data dependency chains reach only two generated hops.

The authors themselves acknowledge some of these limitations, which is commendable.

Concrete fix:

Add experiments varying the following independently:

Maximum dependency depth.

Fraction of generated versus curated triples.

For an arXiv submission, I would not insist that all these experiments be completed, but the performance conclusions should remain explicitly limited to the tested workloads.

W5. The SPARQL-star comparison is narrower than the paper's portability argument

Sections 6.2–6.3

The comparison against ordinary SPARQL-star closure queries is useful. The dedicated implementation is approximately 6–10 times faster in the reported tests.

However, both implementations execute against Loka's own engine.

This establishes that the specialized traversal is faster than the general query executor in this implementation. It does not establish comparative performance against independent RDF-star database implementations.

The statement that any SPARQL-star store can compute the same closure is defensible at the level of query semantics, but practical portability depends on quoted-triple support, property-path behavior, indexes, and query optimization.

The paper even notes that Loka cannot evaluate a property path whose endpoint is a quoted pattern.

Concrete fix:

Describe the comparison explicitly as an internal implementation baseline.

Avoid implying that the measured speedup generalizes to other RDF-star systems.

If feasible, test one independent RDF-star implementation.

Separate semantic portability from performance portability.

5. Minor issues: clarity, terminology, and citations
5.1 Terminology

§§1–3: Selection provenance

The term is defensible, and the authors do a good job distinguishing it from why-provenance.

This should appear in the abstract or immediately after the first introduction of the term.

The phrase suggests three independent security boundaries. In reality, the layers have different responsibilities and some guarantees depend on a particular layer.

The paper calls the annotation block fixed-shape, but the number of propositionSelectedFrom annotations is variable.

Retraction-set computation.

Persistent deletion.

These are currently understandable from context, but consistent terminology would improve the paper.

The confidence value is explicitly described as uncalibrated, which is good.

6. Overall assessment
Weak Accept

The strongest aspect of this paper is its engineering discipline.

It does not try to disguise an unsuccessful link-prediction experiment as an ML contribution. It reports the poor model performance, explains why the generator is not the central contribution, and provides actual implementation and evaluation evidence for the provenance mechanism.

I particularly appreciate three decisions:

Using RDF-star to represent individual statement dependencies rather than introducing a separate metadata subsystem.

Explicitly distinguishing procedural selection provenance from semantic support.

Comparing the specialized retraction implementation with a general SPARQL-star approach rather than simply reporting its own runtime.

The most important weakness is that the paper sometimes moves between three different notions of dependency:

What the model learned during training.

What the inference procedure consulted when proposing a candidate.

What statements the model actually used to produce a particular value.

Only the second is really captured by the current mechanism. The paper knows this, but its broader framing occasionally obscures it.

The other major limitation is evaluation scope. The implementation is convincing for its intended workload, but the experiments do not establish general performance characteristics across different provenance graph structures or independent RDF-star implementations.

Critical peer review: Loka — Provenance for Retracting Model-Generated Triples in an RDF-star Store
Weak Accept

Recommendation for a systems/database venue

1. Summary

The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that records provenance for model-generated triples and uses that provenance to support exclusion from subsequent training corpora and cascading retraction. Its central contribution is a reserved RDF-star annotation schema recording the generating model, confidence score, and selection provenance: the stored statements that caused the inference procedure to propose a particular subject–predicate pair. The system uses these explicit dependency edges to retract generated statements transitively when a source entity is removed, while avoiding traversal through ordinary data relationships. The implementation is evaluated using synthetic dependency graphs and real Wikidata-derived stores, including a 5-million-row synthetic benchmark, a 2-million-triple real-data experiment, and comparisons against SPARQL-star closure queries and alternative RDF provenance encodings. The paper also evaluates its model-generation component against predicate-frequency and TransE baselines, finding that its transformer does not outperform predicate frequency. Importantly, the authors explicitly distinguish procedural provenance from semantic justification: the recorded statements explain why a candidate was proposed, not why the predicted object is correct. Overall, this is a useful systems-engineering contribution with a clearly scoped problem, a concrete implementation, and unusually candid reporting of limitations. Its principal weakness is that the correctness and performance evidence establishes the behavior of one particular bounded selection procedure rather than a general provenance solution for model-generated knowledge graphs.

2. Recommendation
Weak Accept

I would lean toward acceptance as a systems implementation paper, although the contribution is relatively incremental in its underlying algorithms.

Reasons to accept:

The problem is real and clearly motivated: generated knowledge graph statements need to be distinguishable, excluded from training, and retractable when their sources are withdrawn.

The RDF-star representation is straightforward and reasonably elegant. It avoids requiring a separate provenance database or an additional reification layer.

The implementation goes beyond a conceptual schema. It integrates extraction, candidate selection, annotation, inference, and deletion.

The evaluation includes independent reference implementations, actual stores, a SPARQL baseline, and persistent deletion measurements.

The paper is unusually transparent about failure cases, including a correctness defect discovered during evaluation and the fact that the model performs worse than a simple baseline.

Reasons against a stronger recommendation:

The fundamental cascade-retraction algorithm is a specialized dependency-closure traversal, not a substantially new database algorithm.

The provenance semantics are narrower than the terminology might initially suggest.

The evaluation is concentrated on one implementation, one dataset family, and relatively shallow real dependency chains.

The paper does not adequately establish the generality of its performance claims or the completeness of its provenance guarantees outside its particular inference pipeline.

I would not recommend Reject because the paper does deliver a working system and meaningful experimental evidence. However, I would not recommend Accept without qualification because several aspects of the contribution need sharper technical framing.

3. Main weaknesses and concrete fixes
W1. The provenance semantics do not capture the model's actual data dependencies

Major conceptual issue Sections 2.4, 2.6, 3.2, 4.4, 7.2

This is the most important issue in the paper.

The authors carefully distinguish selection provenance from semantic support, which is good. However, there is a deeper distinction that needs to be made explicit: the statements used by the candidate selector are not necessarily the complete set of data dependencies of the generated prediction.

The model is trained on a corpus containing potentially millions of triples. Its parameters can encode information from any of those training examples. At inference time, the model receives only subject and predicate labels, but that does not mean its prediction is independent of the rest of the training corpus.

For example:

A curated Wikidata statement about an entity enters the training corpus.

The transformer learns a statistical association from that statement.

A later prediction uses a candidate selected through an entirely different set of statements.

The selected statements are recorded as provenance.

The original training statement is deleted, but the model's parameters still encode whatever it learned from it.

The retraction procedure will not identify this dependency.

This matters because §2.4 describes cascade retraction as removing a source's influence from model-generated stored outputs, while §2.6 motivates training from scratch on a known corpus partly on the grounds that it keeps the model's learned information within a known dataset.

Those are not equivalent guarantees.

The paper's actual mechanism tracks dependencies of the inference procedure, not dependencies of the model's learned parameters.

Concrete fix:

Explicitly distinguish training-data provenance, candidate-selection provenance, and inference-time input provenance.

State that Loka implements the second category, with a record of the third category's selector inputs.

Clarify that deleting a training example does not remove its influence from an already-trained model.

Narrow the claims in §§2.4 and 2.6 accordingly.

Consider an experiment demonstrating that deleting a source statement does not necessarily eliminate predictions influenced by the model's training on that statement.

I do not consider this a fatal flaw if the contribution is framed as procedural provenance. However, the distinction is central enough that it should be prominent in the abstract and introduction, not merely implicit in the technical discussion.

W2. The retraction guarantees depend on node-level deletion and a bounded selector

Sections 3.4, 4.4, 7.2

The retraction algorithm is presented clearly, but its guarantees are substantially narrower than a general dependency-provenance system.

The selector examines at most 20 subject statements and 20 distinct neighbours. It then records at most one statement per contributing neighbour.

This produces a maximum of 40 citations per prediction, which is a reasonable engineering decision.

However, the resulting completeness guarantee is conditional on the selector's bounded execution and the node-level deletion semantics.

There are two related problems:

First: statement-level deletion.

The paper correctly acknowledges that only one statement per neighbour is recorded. If a different statement belonging to that neighbour is deleted individually, the prediction may remain even though the deleted statement participated in the selection process.

Second: alternative derivations.

If two independent generation procedures produce the same triple, their citation sets merge. The implementation retracts the triple when any cited source disappears.

This is not equivalent to maintaining multiple justifications. A triple with two independent derivations can be deleted even though one derivation remains valid.

The authors acknowledge both limitations in §7.2, but they have implications for the generality of the claimed provenance mechanism.

Concrete fix:

Add a small formal definition of the supported semantics:

Retraction is node-rooted.

Dependencies are OR-style: any cited source disappearing invalidates the generated triple.

There is one merged provenance set per generated triple.

The selector's bounded execution defines the universe of recorded dependencies.

Then distinguish this from statement-level deletion and alternative-derivation-aware truth maintenance.

A particularly useful experiment would compare bounded and unbounded selection on the same dataset, measuring not only annotation volume but also the difference in retraction results.

The paper already reports citation counts of median 9 versus 105 in §4.4. It should also report what additional dependency coverage is lost through bounding, if that can be measured.

Sections 3.1, 3.3, 5.5

The paper repeatedly emphasizes that generated statements cannot re-enter the training corpus.

The implementation has a sensible three-layer design:

The extractor excludes triples marked as generated.

The selector excludes reserved predicates.

The writer refuses reserved predicates.

However, §3.1 explicitly acknowledges that the store accepts arbitrary triples through its HTTP write interface. An external writer can insert a generated statement without the generated flag.

Such a statement can enter a subsequent training corpus.

Consequently, the system does not enforce a general invariant that generated statements cannot enter training. It enforces an invariant for statements correctly annotated by the Loka inference pipeline.

There is also an asymmetry: excluding generated statements depends on the generated flag, whereas excluding system metadata depends on the reserved namespace.

State explicitly that the guarantee applies to outputs written through the instrumented pipeline.

Consider an integration test that inserts an unflagged generated triple and demonstrates the current behavior.

If the intended guarantee is stronger, introduce a store-level write policy or require an explicit provenance classification for externally generated statements.

The current design is defensible, but the distinction between pipeline enforcement and store enforcement should be made unmistakable.

Critical peer review: Loka — Provenance for Retracting Model-Generated Triples in an RDF-star Store
Weak Accept

Recommendation for a systems/database venue

1. Summary

The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that records provenance for model-generated triples and uses that provenance to support exclusion from subsequent training corpora and cascading retraction. Its central contribution is a reserved RDF-star annotation schema recording the generating model, confidence score, and selection provenance: the stored statements that caused the inference procedure to propose a particular subject–predicate pair. The system uses these explicit dependency edges to retract generated statements transitively when a source entity is removed, while avoiding traversal through ordinary data relationships. The implementation is evaluated using synthetic dependency graphs and real Wikidata-derived stores, including a 5-million-row synthetic benchmark, a 2-million-triple real-data experiment, and comparisons against SPARQL-star closure queries and alternative RDF provenance encodings. The paper also evaluates its model-generation component against predicate-frequency and TransE baselines, finding that its transformer does not outperform predicate frequency. Importantly, the authors explicitly distinguish procedural provenance from semantic justification: the recorded statements explain why a candidate was proposed, not why the predicted object is correct. Overall, this is a useful systems-engineering contribution with a clearly scoped problem, a concrete implementation, and unusually candid reporting of limitations. Its principal weakness is that the correctness and performance evidence establishes the behavior of one particular bounded selection procedure rather than a general provenance solution for model-generated knowledge graphs.

2. Recommendation
Weak Accept

I would lean toward acceptance as a systems implementation paper, although the contribution is relatively incremental in its underlying algorithms.

Reasons to accept:

The problem is real and clearly motivated: generated knowledge graph statements need to be distinguishable, excluded from training, and retractable when their sources are withdrawn.

The RDF-star representation is straightforward and reasonably elegant. It avoids requiring a separate provenance database or an additional reification layer.

The implementation goes beyond a conceptual schema. It integrates extraction, candidate selection, annotation, inference, and deletion.

The evaluation includes independent reference implementations, actual stores, a SPARQL baseline, and persistent deletion measurements.

The paper is unusually transparent about failure cases, including a correctness defect discovered during evaluation and the fact that the model performs worse than a simple baseline.

Reasons against a stronger recommendation:

The fundamental cascade-retraction algorithm is a specialized dependency-closure traversal, not a substantially new database algorithm.

The provenance semantics are narrower than the terminology might initially suggest.

The evaluation is concentrated on one implementation, one dataset family, and relatively shallow real dependency chains.

The paper does not adequately establish the generality of its performance claims or the completeness of its provenance guarantees outside its particular inference pipeline.

I would not recommend Reject because the paper does deliver a working system and meaningful experimental evidence. However, I would not recommend Accept without qualification because several aspects of the contribution need sharper technical framing.

3. Main weaknesses and concrete fixes
W1. The provenance semantics do not capture the model's actual data dependencies

Major conceptual issue Sections 2.4, 2.6, 3.2, 4.4, 7.2

This is the most important issue in the paper.

The authors carefully distinguish selection provenance from semantic support, which is good. However, there is a deeper distinction that needs to be made explicit: the statements used by the candidate selector are not necessarily the complete set of data dependencies of the generated prediction.

The model is trained on a corpus containing potentially millions of triples. Its parameters can encode information from any of those training examples. At inference time, the model receives only subject and predicate labels, but that does not mean its prediction is independent of the rest of the training corpus.

For example:

A curated Wikidata statement about an entity enters the training corpus.

The transformer learns a statistical association from that statement.

A later prediction uses a candidate selected through an entirely different set of statements.

The selected statements are recorded as provenance.

The original training statement is deleted, but the model's parameters still encode whatever it learned from it.

The retraction procedure will not identify this dependency.

This matters because §2.4 describes cascade retraction as removing a source's influence from model-generated stored outputs, while §2.6 motivates training from scratch on a known corpus partly on the grounds that it keeps the model's learned information within a known dataset.

Those are not equivalent guarantees.

The paper's actual mechanism tracks dependencies of the inference procedure, not dependencies of the model's learned parameters.

Concrete fix:

Explicitly distinguish training-data provenance, candidate-selection provenance, and inference-time input provenance.

State that Loka implements the second category, with a record of the third category's selector inputs.

Clarify that deleting a training example does not remove its influence from an already-trained model.

Narrow the claims in §§2.4 and 2.6 accordingly.

Consider an experiment demonstrating that deleting a source statement does not necessarily eliminate predictions influenced by the model's training on that statement.

I do not consider this a fatal flaw if the contribution is framed as procedural provenance. However, the distinction is central enough that it should be prominent in the abstract and introduction, not merely implicit in the technical discussion.

W2. The retraction guarantees depend on node-level deletion and a bounded selector

Sections 3.4, 4.4, 7.2

The retraction algorithm is presented clearly, but its guarantees are substantially narrower than a general dependency-provenance system.

The selector examines at most 20 subject statements and 20 distinct neighbours. It then records at most one statement per contributing neighbour.

This produces a maximum of 40 citations per prediction, which is a reasonable engineering decision.

However, the resulting completeness guarantee is conditional on the selector's bounded execution and the node-level deletion semantics.

There are two related problems:

First: statement-level deletion.

The paper correctly acknowledges that only one statement per neighbour is recorded. If a different statement belonging to that neighbour is deleted individually, the prediction may remain even though the deleted statement participated in the selection process.

Second: alternative derivations.

If two independent generation procedures produce the same triple, their citation sets merge. The implementation retracts the triple when any cited source disappears.

This is not equivalent to maintaining multiple justifications. A triple with two independent derivations can be deleted even though one derivation remains valid.

The authors acknowledge both limitations in §7.2, but they have implications for the generality of the claimed provenance mechanism.

Concrete fix:

Add a small formal definition of the supported semantics:

Retraction is node-rooted.

Dependencies are OR-style: any cited source disappearing invalidates the generated triple.

There is one merged provenance set per generated triple.

The selector's bounded execution defines the universe of recorded dependencies.

Then distinguish this from statement-level deletion and alternative-derivation-aware truth maintenance.

A particularly useful experiment would compare bounded and unbounded selection on the same dataset, measuring not only annotation volume but also the difference in retraction results.

The paper already reports citation counts of median 9 versus 105 in §4.4. It should also report what additional dependency coverage is lost through bounding, if that can be measured.

W3. The training exclusion guarantee is a pipeline property, not a store invariant

Sections 3.1, 3.3, 5.5

The paper repeatedly emphasizes that generated statements cannot re-enter the training corpus.

The implementation has a sensible three-layer design:

The extractor excludes triples marked as generated.

The selector excludes reserved predicates.

The writer refuses reserved predicates.

However, §3.1 explicitly acknowledges that the store accepts arbitrary triples through its HTTP write interface. An external writer can insert a generated statement without the generated flag.

Such a statement can enter a subsequent training corpus.

Consequently, the system does not enforce a general invariant that generated statements cannot enter training. It enforces an invariant for statements correctly annotated by the Loka inference pipeline.

There is also an asymmetry: excluding generated statements depends on the generated flag, whereas excluding system metadata depends on the reserved namespace.

Concrete fix:

State explicitly that the guarantee applies to outputs written through the instrumented pipeline.

Consider an integration test that inserts an unflagged generated triple and demonstrates the current behavior.

If the intended guarantee is stronger, introduce a store-level write policy or require an explicit provenance classification for externally generated statements.

The current design is defensible, but the distinction between pipeline enforcement and store enforcement should be made unmistakable.

W4. The evaluation does not establish general scalability of the retraction algorithm

Sections 6.1–6.2

The performance evaluation is one of the stronger parts of the paper, but it is not sufficient to support broad scalability claims.

The synthetic benchmark is useful:

The synthetic dependency generator does not establish that real-world provenance graphs have comparable degree distributions.

W5. The SPARQL-star comparison is narrower than the paper's portability argument

Sections 6.2–6.3

The comparison against ordinary SPARQL-star closure queries is useful. The dedicated implementation is approximately 6–10 times faster in the reported tests.

However, both implementations execute against Loka's own engine.

This establishes that the specialized traversal is faster than the general query executor in this implementation. It does not establish comparative performance against independent RDF-star database implementations.

The statement that any SPARQL-star store can compute the same closure is defensible at the level of query semantics, but practical portability depends on quoted-triple support, property-path behavior, indexes, and query optimization.

The paper even notes that Loka cannot evaluate a property path whose endpoint is a quoted pattern.

Concrete fix:

Describe the comparison explicitly as an internal implementation baseline.

Avoid implying that the measured speedup generalizes to other RDF-star systems.

If feasible, test one independent RDF-star implementation.

Separate semantic portability from performance portability.

Sections 5, 6.4, 7.1, 7.3

The paper deserves credit for reporting that the transformer does not outperform predicate frequency.

However, the evaluation has limitations that affect how much can be concluded:

Only one checkpoint, v13, is evaluated.

There is no validation split.

Neither learned model is tuned.

The held-out data is restricted to candidates already observed with the predicate.

The evaluation is transductive and uses English labels as entity identifiers.

The transformer scores candidates using summed token log-probabilities, which may introduce sequence-length effects.

This limits the immediate usefulness of the generator as a knowledge graph completion system.

Explicitly position the model as an experimental workload generator.

Clarify that the link-prediction benchmark evaluates a restricted candidate-ranking problem.

Explain the possible sequence-length bias in the scoring method.

Avoid implying that the evaluation validates the quality of the generated knowledge.

The existing limitations section does much of this already.

The paper proposes storing model-generated triples in an RDF-star store together with a fixed block of annotations in a reserved namespace (generated flag, model version, decoding confidence, and propositionSelectedFrom edges pointing at the stored statements the candidate-selection heuristic consumed). Two operational uses are built on this: (i) a corpus extractor that filters generated triples and reserved-namespace rows so model output does not re-enter training data, and (ii) node-rooted cascade retraction that follows only propositionSelectedFrom edges to remove transitively dependent generated triples. The engine is the author’s own Rust store (Loka). Correctness of retract_set is checked against a fixpoint reference on synthetic graphs (700 roots) and against an independently computed closure on two real Wikidata stores (153k and 2M triples, two generated hops); cost is ~0.7–0.8 µs per removed triple on the large synthetic stores and 6–10× faster than an equivalent SPARQL-star closure. An encoding comparison against reification+PROV-O and named graphs shows 2.8×/2.4× fewer rows. The generator used throughout is a 44.5M-parameter from-scratch masked-triple transformer that does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline on held-out link prediction; the paper is explicit that its claims rest on the provenance machinery, not the model.

2. Recommendation

Weak Reject for a main-track systems/databases venue; would be a solid Accept at a workshop (e.g., TaPP, a KG/provenance workshop) with the fixes below. The engineering is careful and the paper is unusually honest about its limits, but the technical novelty is thin (annotation schema + a DRed-without-counting closure, which the paper itself concedes in §2.5 and §6.2), the central mechanism of Contribution 1 is never empirically exercised, and the evaluation never compares to an existing RDF-star store. Nothing here blocks an arXiv posting; the comments are aimed at what a venue reviewer would raise.

3. Main weaknesses

W1. Contribution 1 (corpus exclusion) is never tested, and the “closed loop” was not actually closed for the models evaluated. (§3.1, §3.3, §5.5, §6)
Every real-data experiment uses v13. Per §5.5 and Appendix A, v11–v14 were trained on corpora streamed directly from the source parquet, not extracted from a store. So the SPARQL-star FILTER NOT EXISTS of §3.1 played no role in producing any model in the paper, and no experiment ever (a) posts generated triples into a store, (b) runs the extractor, and (c) verifies the corpus contains zero generated triples and zero reserved rows. The §5.5 sentence “the provenance guarantee of §3.1 is unchanged” is vacuous on the streaming path—generated triples are absent from the source dump by construction.
Fix: add a small, explicit experiment: take the 153k store after the two inference passes (356 generated triples), run the store-based extractor, report the counts of generated/reserved rows in the output (should be 0/0), and repeat with the generated-flag filter disabled to show the leak size. Also train at least one model (even a tiny one) on a store-extracted corpus that contained generated triples at extraction time, so Contribution 4’s “exercises the loop end to end” is literally true.

W2. No comparison with, or implementation on, an existing RDF-star store. (§3, §6.2, §6.3)
§6.2 shows the retraction set is computable with standard SPARQL-star queries, and the paper then states “any SPARQL-star store that holds the annotation block can compute the same retraction set.” This simultaneously undercuts the need for a new engine and goes untested—no second store was tried. A DB audience will ask why the schema wasn’t deployed on Oxigraph, Jena, GraphDB, or Stardog (all of which support RDF-star) and benchmarked there. §4.2’s note that Loka’s own SPARQL serialization embeds datatype IRIs inside literal strings is a conformance bug in the engine being presented, and it weakens the engine as a contribution.
Fix: either run the §6.2 SPARQL-star closure on one off-the-shelf RDF-star store (same graphs, same roots) and report agreement and latency, or reposition the paper as a schema-and-policy contribution and drop the engine claims. Fix the datatype serialization in the engine rather than working around it in preprocessing.

W3. Retraction cost claim rests on two data points and is contradicted by the small rows. (§6.2, Abstract, §9)
The paper says cost follows removal-set size, not store size, but per-removed-triple cost rises from 0.31 µs to 0.80 µs across the four rows, and the two “large” rows differ in both store size (10×) and depth (34 vs 39) while having similar removal sizes. The paper admits this, but the abstract and conclusion still carry the headline.
Fix: a controlled sweep—fix removal-set size (choose roots by closure size) and vary store size over ≥4 points; separately fix store size and vary depth. Report per-triple cost vs. depth. Also report hardware (CPU model, RAM, whether sled is on SSD); “single laptop” is not reproducible.

W4. Depth-0 definition may miss curated annotation rows as citable statements. (§3.4, §4.4)
R0 is “triples with n as subject or object.” Wikidata qualifier/reference rows have a quoted triple as subject, so a row <<n p o>> pq:x y is not in R0 under that definition. If the selector ever consults such rows as “the subject’s statements,” a generated triple citing one would not be reached. The paper never states whether the selector excludes non-reserved annotation rows.
Fix: state explicitly whether the selector’s “statements of the subject” includes annotation rows; if not, say so and add a unit test; if so, extend R0 to rows whose quoted subject touches n.

W5. The held-out set construction is described two different ways. (§6.4 vs §7.3)
§6.4: held-out = triples in v14-1M that v13 never trained on, transductively filtered. §7.3: held-out = “the triples a larger label cache newly resolved.” Appendix A shows v14’s corpus is ~1.5M triples larger than v13’s, yet only 28,448 survive—the filter doing that work is never named. Readers cannot reconstruct the split.
Fix: give the exact construction as a pipeline (source rows → candidate triples → each filter with counts) and release the held-out file.

W6. §6.5 tests something that is nearly true by construction. (§4.4, §6.5)
Step 1 (selection) runs before the model and does not read model output, so per-prediction citation statistics being generator-independent follows from the code structure. The only generator-dependent channels are the emit threshold and the second pass. The section is still useful for the chained-dependency stress (3,818 second-pass citations), but it should be framed as that, not as evidence of “independence.”
Fix: reframe as a scale/chaining test, and state up front that selection precedes generation.

W7. Too much model-debugging history for a cs.DB paper. (§5, Appendix B)
~3 pages (§5.2–5.4, Appendix B) describe datatype leakage, catalog noise and BPE artifacts of a model the paper explicitly says is not the contribution. Combined with the propositionInferredFrom→propositionSelectedFrom rename note (§3.1), the “found redundant” note on propositionImportedFrom, and “earlier versions used a cruder rule” (§7.2), the paper reads partly as a changelog.
Fix: compress §5 to half a page, move Appendix B to the repository, and drop rename/history notes except the one sentence needed to read the released stores.

W8. The three-layer enforcement paragraph is internally inconsistent. (§3.1, Contribution 1)
Contribution 1 says the model “can neither learn nor emit system metadata even if one of those guards regresses.” §3.1 then states that keeping annotation rows out of training “rests on the extractor’s prefix filter alone,” and keeping generated triples out “rests on the extractor’s generated-flag filter alone.” So the “learn” half has one guard, not three. The paragraph also says the selector/emit guards “are not covered by a test that disables the other.”
Fix: restate as: output side is double-guarded; input (training) side is single-guarded. Add the two missing mutual-disable tests.

Abstract, sentence beginning “Tested against an independent reference…” conflates two experiments. The fixpoint reference (§6.1) was run on graphs of ≤4,000 triples; the 5M-row timing graph was checked only against the SPARQL-star closure through the same engine’s executor (§6.2). Say which check applies to which number.
§6.2, 2M store: the row arithmetic does not reconcile from the numbers given. 2,000,623 imported + 672 generated + 13,318 annotation rows = 2,014,613; minus 5,377 committed removals = 2,009,236, not the reported 2,009,885 (difference 649). Either the pre-retraction row count, the count of propositionPredictedLabel rows, importer rejections at this scale, or whether the 30 commits were on a copy is unstated. Give the full ledger.
§6.1 and §3.2 vs. the §3.1 table: §6.1 says “§3.2 also lists the generated flag, confidence and predicted label,” but the §3.2 block does not include propositionPredictedLabel; only the §3.1 table and §4.4 step 4 do. Make §3.2’s block the canonical one and include the optional row.
§2.6 claims everything the model learned is “inside a known, released dataset,” but §4.2 fetches missing property labels from the live Wikidata SPARQL endpoint, and §7.3 says the source revision was not pinned. The claim should be qualified.
§6.2 “any SPARQL-star store… can compute the same retraction set with standard queries” is asserted after noting the engine itself could not evaluate the natural property path and needed a rewrite. Untested on any other store; say “in principle.”

§6.1 “about 5% also cite a later generated triple so that the citation graph contains cycles”: citing a later triple does not by itself create a cycle. §4.1: collapsing pq:/pr: onto wdt: on annotation rows loses the qualifier/reference distinction and Wikidata’s reference grouping (several pr: triples share one reference node). Say what is lost.
§2.1: quoted_triple_id is “a hash of the three component ids”—state the hash width and collision handling.
§4.4 step 2: the penalty formula renders as penaltycount[t]; ensure the exponent is typeset. Also note it divides probabilities, not logits as in Keskar et al.
“Preprint.” appears stranded at the top of page 2.
