Review: “Loka: Provenance for Retracting Model-Generated Triples in an RDF-star Store”

1. Summary

The paper proposes storing model-generated triples in an RDF-star store together with a fixed block of annotations in a reserved namespace (generated flag, model version, decoding confidence, and propositionSelectedFrom edges pointing at the stored statements the candidate-selection heuristic consumed). Two operational uses are built on this: (i) a corpus extractor that filters generated triples and reserved-namespace rows so model output does not re-enter training data, and (ii) node-rooted cascade retraction that follows only propositionSelectedFrom edges to remove transitively dependent generated triples. The engine is the author’s own Rust store (Loka). Correctness of retract_set is checked against a fixpoint reference on synthetic graphs (700 roots) and against an independently computed closure on two real Wikidata stores (153k and 2M triples, two generated hops); cost is ~0.7–0.8 µs per removed triple on the large synthetic stores and 6–10× faster than an equivalent SPARQL-star closure. An encoding comparison against reification+PROV-O and named graphs shows 2.8×/2.4× fewer rows. The generator used throughout is a 44.5M-parameter from-scratch masked-triple transformer that does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline on held-out link prediction; the paper is explicit that its claims rest on the provenance machinery, not the model.

2. Recommendation

Weak Reject for a main-track systems/databases venue; would be a solid Accept at a workshop (e.g., TaPP, a KG/provenance workshop) with the fixes below. The engineering is careful and the paper is unusually honest about its limits, but the technical novelty is thin (annotation schema + a DRed-without-counting closure, which the paper itself concedes in §2.5 and §6.2), the central mechanism of Contribution 1 is never empirically exercised, and the evaluation never compares to an existing RDF-star store. Nothing here blocks an arXiv posting; the comments are aimed at what a venue reviewer would raise.

3. Main weaknesses

W1. Contribution 1 (corpus exclusion) is never tested, and the “closed loop” was not actually closed for the models evaluated. (§3.1, §3.3, §5.5, §6)
Every real-data experiment uses v13. Per §5.5 and Appendix A, v11–v14 were trained on corpora streamed directly from the source parquet, not extracted from a store. So the SPARQL-star FILTER NOT EXISTS of §3.1 played no role in producing any model in the paper, and no experiment ever (a) posts generated triples into a store, (b) runs the extractor, and (c) verifies the corpus contains zero generated triples and zero reserved rows. The §5.5 sentence “the provenance guarantee of §3.1 is unchanged” is vacuous on the streaming path—generated triples are absent from the source dump by construction.
Fix: add a small, explicit experiment: take the 153k store after the two inference passes (356 generated triples), run the store-based extractor, report the counts of generated/reserved rows in the output (should be 0/0), and repeat with the generated-flag filter disabled to show the leak size. Also train at least one model (even a tiny one) on a store-extracted corpus that contained generated triples at extraction time, so Contribution 4’s “exercises the loop end to end” is literally true.

W2. No comparison with, or implementation on, an existing RDF-star store. (§3, §6.2, §6.3)
§6.2 shows the retraction set is computable with standard SPARQL-star queries, and the paper then states “any SPARQL-star store that holds the annotation block can compute the same retraction set.” This simultaneously undercuts the need for a new engine and goes untested—no second store was tried. A DB audience will ask why the schema wasn’t deployed on Oxigraph, Jena, GraphDB, or Stardog (all of which support RDF-star) and benchmarked there. §4.2’s note that Loka’s own SPARQL serialization embeds datatype IRIs inside literal strings is a conformance bug in the engine being presented, and it weakens the engine as a contribution.
Fix: either run the §6.2 SPARQL-star closure on one off-the-shelf RDF-star store (same graphs, same roots) and report agreement and latency, or reposition the paper as a schema-and-policy contribution and drop the engine claims. Fix the datatype serialization in the engine rather than working around it in preprocessing.

W3. Retraction cost claim rests on two data points and is contradicted by the small rows. (§6.2, Abstract, §9)
The paper says cost follows removal-set size, not store size, but per-removed-triple cost rises from 0.31 µs to 0.80 µs across the four rows, and the two “large” rows differ in both store size (10×) and depth (34 vs 39) while having similar removal sizes. The paper admits this, but the abstract and conclusion still carry the headline.
Fix: a controlled sweep—fix removal-set size (choose roots by closure size) and vary store size over ≥4 points; separately fix store size and vary depth. Report per-triple cost vs. depth. Also report hardware (CPU model, RAM, whether sled is on SSD); “single laptop” is not reproducible.

W4. Depth-0 definition may miss curated annotation rows as citable statements. (§3.4, §4.4)
R0 is “triples with n as subject or object.” Wikidata qualifier/reference rows have a quoted triple as subject, so a row <<n p o>> pq:x y is not in R0 under that definition. If the selector ever consults such rows as “the subject’s statements,” a generated triple citing one would not be reached. The paper never states whether the selector excludes non-reserved annotation rows.
Fix: state explicitly whether the selector’s “statements of the subject” includes annotation rows; if not, say so and add a unit test; if so, extend R0 to rows whose quoted subject touches n.

W5. The held-out set construction is described two different ways. (§6.4 vs §7.3)
§6.4: held-out = triples in v14-1M that v13 never trained on, transductively filtered. §7.3: held-out = “the triples a larger label cache newly resolved.” Appendix A shows v14’s corpus is ~1.5M triples larger than v13’s, yet only 28,448 survive—the filter doing that work is never named. Readers cannot reconstruct the split.
Fix: give the exact construction as a pipeline (source rows → candidate triples → each filter with counts) and release the held-out file.

W6. §6.5 tests something that is nearly true by construction. (§4.4, §6.5)
Step 1 (selection) runs before the model and does not read model output, so per-prediction citation statistics being generator-independent follows from the code structure. The only generator-dependent channels are the emit threshold and the second pass. The section is still useful for the chained-dependency stress (3,818 second-pass citations), but it should be framed as that, not as evidence of “independence.”
Fix: reframe as a scale/chaining test, and state up front that selection precedes generation.

W7. Too much model-debugging history for a cs.DB paper. (§5, Appendix B)
~3 pages (§5.2–5.4, Appendix B) describe datatype leakage, catalog noise and BPE artifacts of a model the paper explicitly says is not the contribution. Combined with the propositionInferredFrom→propositionSelectedFrom rename note (§3.1), the “found redundant” note on propositionImportedFrom, and “earlier versions used a cruder rule” (§7.2), the paper reads partly as a changelog.
Fix: compress §5 to half a page, move Appendix B to the repository, and drop rename/history notes except the one sentence needed to read the released stores.

W8. The three-layer enforcement paragraph is internally inconsistent. (§3.1, Contribution 1)
Contribution 1 says the model “can neither learn nor emit system metadata even if one of those guards regresses.” §3.1 then states that keeping annotation rows out of training “rests on the extractor’s prefix filter alone,” and keeping generated triples out “rests on the extractor’s generated-flag filter alone.” So the “learn” half has one guard, not three. The paragraph also says the selector/emit guards “are not covered by a test that disables the other.”
Fix: restate as: output side is double-guarded; input (training) side is single-guarded. Add the two missing mutual-disable tests.

4. Overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent claims
Abstract, sentence beginning “Tested against an independent reference…” conflates two experiments. The fixpoint reference (§6.1) was run on graphs of ≤4,000 triples; the 5M-row timing graph was checked only against the SPARQL-star closure through the same engine’s executor (§6.2). Say which check applies to which number.
§6.2, 2M store: the row arithmetic does not reconcile from the numbers given. 2,000,623 imported + 672 generated + 13,318 annotation rows = 2,014,613; minus 5,377 committed removals = 2,009,236, not the reported 2,009,885 (difference 649). Either the pre-retraction row count, the count of propositionPredictedLabel rows, importer rejections at this scale, or whether the 30 commits were on a copy is unstated. Give the full ledger.
§6.1 and §3.2 vs. the §3.1 table: §6.1 says “§3.2 also lists the generated flag, confidence and predicted label,” but the §3.2 block does not include propositionPredictedLabel; only the §3.1 table and §4.4 step 4 do. Make §3.2’s block the canonical one and include the optional row.
§2.6 claims everything the model learned is “inside a known, released dataset,” but §4.2 fetches missing property labels from the live Wikidata SPARQL endpoint, and §7.3 says the source revision was not pinned. The claim should be qualified.
§6.2 “any SPARQL-star store… can compute the same retraction set with standard queries” is asserted after noting the engine itself could not evaluate the natural property path and needed a rewrite. Untested on any other store; say “in principle.”
§6.3 uses prov:wasDerivedFrom for the reified baseline, while §2.2 argues prov:used is the correct PROV-O relation for selection provenance. The baseline should use the mapping the paper itself recommends.
§6.3 baselines are the most verbose possible encodings: named graphs do not require reifying cited statements (a singleton graph per cited statement costs one quad). The 2.8×/2.4× figures are therefore an upper bound on the advantage; and 38 generated triples is a very small sample. State both.
§6.1 “about 5% also cite a later generated triple so that the citation graph contains cycles”: citing a later triple does not by itself create a cycle. Also note that in production the citation graph is acyclic by write-time causality, so the cycle test is a robustness check, not a production scenario.
§3.4 “Statement-level retraction would need two changes,” then the first item explains the closure already works per triple—i.e., it is not a change. One change.
§6.2 inference cost grows from ~1 s to ~5 s per subject between the 153k and 2M stores. Since the model is fixed, this is the neighbour selector scaling with store size—a loop-scalability concern that deserves one sentence rather than being left as an aside.
5. Minor issues

Terminology / notation

The prefix prov: is used for http://loka.dev/provenance/ (§3.2) and, by convention and in §2.2/§6.3, for PROV-O. This is actively confusing in a provenance paper. Use loka: or lp:.
“Quoted triple” follows the CG report; the W3C RDF-star WG (RDF 1.2) has moved to “triple terms” with rdf:reifies and changed the asserted/unasserted semantics, which bears directly on the §7.2 claim that annotating an unasserted quoted triple is well-formed. Cite the RDF 1.2 WG drafts and say which model you follow.
§4.1: collapsing pq:/pr: onto wdt: on annotation rows loses the qualifier/reference distinction and Wikidata’s reference grouping (several pr: triples share one reference node). Say what is lost.
§2.1: quoted_triple_id is “a hash of the three component ids”—state the hash width and collision handling.
§4.4 step 2: the penalty formula renders as penaltycount[t]; ensure the exponent is typeset. Also note it divides probabilities, not logits as in Keskar et al.
“Preprint.” appears stranded at the top of page 2.
§8 “Discussion” is future work; title it so.

Related work gaps

Wikidata’s own modelling of machine-derived statements (reference properties such as “inferred from” / “based on heuristic”) is the closest deployed precedent and is not mentioned.
Deletion propagation through views (Buneman, Khanna, Tan 2002) and provenance-aware deletion in annotated-DB systems (e.g., ProvSQL/Perm line) belong next to Gupta et al. in §2.5.
Existing RDF-star-capable stores (Oxigraph, Jena, GraphDB, Stardog) should be named in §2.1 given W2.

Evaluation reporting

No hardware specification anywhere.
§6.4: sum-of-token-log-probs scoring penalises long candidates; mean-per-token or length-normalised scoring is the usual choice and may change the ranking vs. predicate frequency. Not central, but one line.
§6.2 and B.2 use two different Q42 neighbourhoods (14,819/169 vs 14,586/183) plus a third in §6.2 (155,324/983). Give each a name.
§7.3’s “only one checkpoint (v13) has a held-out set” should be stated in §6.4, not only in limitations.

Citations

References are correct as far as I can tell; add Hartig’s later SPARQL-star semantics work and the RDF 1.2 WG specs. The TripleProv citation is fine; consider also citing its follow-up on provenance-aware query execution if the engine claims expand.

If you want, I can turn this into a doc you can hand to a co-reviewer or keep alongside the revision.

---
Peer Review of cs.DB arXiv Paper
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf
You

You are a critical peer reviewer for a systems/databases venue. Review the attached paper, which is about to be submitted to arXiv (cs.DB). Give: (1) a one-paragraph summary; (2) a recommendation (Strong Accept / Accept / Weak Accept / Weak Reject / Reject); (3) the main weaknesses, each with the section it concerns and a concrete fix; (4) any claims that are overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent with the paper's own tables; (5) minor issues (clarity, terminology, citations). Be specific and cite section numbers.

Grok
Worked for 20s

1. One-paragraph summary

Loka is an RDF-star triplestore that stores model-generated triples beside curated data and annotates each generated triple, in a reserved namespace, with the generating model, a confidence score, and “selection provenance” edges (quoted pointers to the stored statements the prediction procedure actually consulted when proposing the (subject, predicate) slot). The design enforces three layers of exclusion so that neither generated triples nor system annotations re-enter training corpora, and supports cascade retraction that follows only the selection-provenance edges (never ordinary data edges) to remove a node and every generated triple that transitively depended on any of its statements. The machinery is exercised end-to-end with a series of small from-scratch masked-triple transformers on cleaned Wikidata slices; retraction is validated against an independent reference (finding and fixing one defect), timed on synthetic stores up to 5 M rows and real Wikidata stores of 153 k and 2 M triples with two-hop chains, compared for storage cost against reification and named graphs, and shown to be independent of the particular generator. The authors are explicit that the case-study model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline and that their claims concern only the provenance machinery.

2. Recommendation

Weak Accept

The problem is real and increasingly relevant, the use of RDF-star is clean, the distinction between selection provenance and support/why-provenance is carefully drawn, the exclusion and retraction mechanisms are well-specified and instrumented, and the evaluation of the retraction engine itself is honest and thorough. The paper is also unusually careful not to over-claim on the model. However, the core technical contribution is the operationalisation of a relatively standard dependency-tracking idea inside an RDF-star store with pipeline guards; the case-study generator is weak, the real-data chains are shallow, and the evaluation does not yet stress the system at a scale or with a workload that would make the engineering contribution decisive for a competitive systems/databases venue.

3. Main weaknesses

Limited novelty relative to the systems contribution claimed (Sections 1–3, 2.5, 8). Once RDF-star is available, attaching a fixed annotation block and performing a restricted graph closure for cascade deletion is a natural engineering step. The paper correctly situates itself against truth-maintenance systems, view-maintenance, TripleProv, PROV-O and nanopublications, and it is careful about what “selection provenance” does not mean. Still, the distinctive technical content is mainly the three-layer exclusion discipline, the bounded selector, and the reserved-namespace invariant.
Concrete fix: Either (a) deepen the comparison to an existing production RDF store with native provenance or reification support (query cost, update cost, storage) under a realistic mixed curated/generated workload, or (b) add one stronger mechanism (e.g., statement-level retraction with multi-statement citations, or an ontology-driven selector as sketched in Section 8) and evaluate it.
End-to-end loop is exercised only with a weak generator (Sections 5, 6.2, 6.4, 6.5, 7.1). The authors are transparent that the v13 transformer does not beat predicate frequency on the held-out split (Section 6.4) and that the machinery is independent of the generator (Section 6.5). Nevertheless, the real-data retraction experiments use only a few hundred generated triples and two hops; the frequency baseline produces far more triples but still only the same shallow chains. The system is therefore never stressed by a strong, high-volume, multi-hop generator.
Concrete fix: Re-run the two-pass pipeline of Section 6.2 with a stronger off-the-shelf link predictor (or even a simple rule-based generator that produces longer chains) and report both retraction correctness and the resulting citation-graph statistics. Even a modest increase in chain depth and volume would make the cost and correctness claims more persuasive.
Retraction is node-rooted and the citation record is deliberately incomplete (Sections 3.4, 4.4, 7.2). The paper correctly notes that statement-level retraction would require citing every matching statement of each neighbour (median 105 citations instead of 9) and that the current design over-deletes when identical triples are written with separate annotation blocks. These are real limitations for any store that mixes curated and generated data. The decision to leave curated qualifier/reference annotations behind is also acknowledged, but it leaves the store in a state that many applications would consider inconsistent.
Concrete fix: Either implement and measure statement-level retraction (with the unbounded or multi-citation selector) on the same real stores, or add a short quantitative analysis of how often the current one-statement-per-neighbour approximation would miss a dependency under a plausible statement-deletion workload.
Scale and workload remain modest for a systems paper (Section 6.2). Synthetic stores reach 5 M rows and real stores 2 M triples, but inference covers only a sample of 3 000 subjects on the larger store, chains are depth 2, and absolute times are from a single laptop. The SPARQL-star baseline is a useful sanity check, yet there is no comparison against a production triplestore’s reification or named-graph implementation under concurrent reads/writes.
Concrete fix: At minimum, report the same retraction preview and commit numbers on a larger real extract (or a deeper synthetic chain) and add one concurrent-query micro-benchmark while retraction is running. You are a critical peer reviewer for a systems/databases venue. Review the attached paper, which is about to be submitted to arXiv (cs.DB). Give: (1) a one-paragraph summary; (2) a recommendation (Strong Accept / Accept / Weak Accept / Weak Reject / Reject); (3) the main weaknesses, each with the section it concerns and a concrete fix; (4) any claims that are overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent with the paper's own tables; (5) minor issues (clarity, terminology, citations). Be specific and cite section numbers.

6:51pm
Thought for 7s
Review: "Loka: Provenance for Retracting Model-Generated Triples in an RDF-star Store"
(1) Summary

The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that stores model-generated triples alongside curated ones, annotated in a reserved namespace (propositionGenerated, propositionGeneratedBy, propositionConfidence, propositionSelectedFrom) with quoted-triple pointers to the statements the prediction procedure consumed ("selection provenance"). Because dependencies are explicit graph edges, the store supports node-rooted cascade retraction, and three pipeline guards keep generated triples and system metadata out of training corpora. The loop is exercised end-to-end with a series of from-scratch transformers (v3–v14) on label-substituted Wikidata. Retraction is validated against an independent reference on synthetic graphs (up to 5M rows) and on real 153k and 2M-triple stores; it is 6–10× faster than an equivalent SPARQL-star closure. The authors are candid that the model itself is weak — below a predicate-frequency baseline — and scope their claims to the provenance machinery.

(2) Recommendation: Weak Accept

The problem is real and timely, the mechanism is concrete and tested against an independent reference (which found a genuine defect, a good sign of honest evaluation), and the artifact release is exemplary. But the evaluation is thin in places the claims depend on (scaling, calibration, third-party writers), and the case-study model adds 5 pages of debugging narrative whose contribution to the core claim is limited. A systems venue should value the operational provenance/retraction design, but the paper overreaches in a few places detailed below.

(3) Main weaknesses (with fixes)

W1 — Scaling claim rests on two points (§6.2). The conclusion states cost "follows the size of the removal rather than of the store," but the paper itself concedes this is "two data points," and the 100k store removes more triples (120,461) than the 1M store (106,255), so the confound is not even controlled. The per-triple cost also varies 0.31–0.8 µs unexplained. Fix: run a proper 2-D grid — store size × removal size (e.g., 4 store sizes × 4 root choices with known removal-set sizes) and report a fit; even 20 cells on a laptop would settle it.

W2 — The corpus-exclusion invariant is enforced in the pipeline, not the store (§3.1). The abstract's "the pipeline's own outputs never re-enter a training corpus" is unconditional, but §3.1 admits the store accepts any triple via POST /triples, so a generated triple written by any other tool without the flag silently enters the next corpus. For a store paper this is the central invariant, and it is guaranteed only by convention. Fix: either add a store-level mode requiring generated flags on (or provenance blocks for) writes from designated "generated" writers, or state the trust model explicitly in the abstract and §3.1.

W3 — Statement-level retraction is incompleteness papered over by node-granularity (§3.4, §7.2). Citing one statement per contributing neighbour means a single-statement deletion (or correction) would miss dependencies; the "merged citations over-delete" issue (§7.2) is a real correctness gap vs. counting derivations (Gupta et al., 1993). Both are acknowledged but left as limitations. Fix: at minimum, evaluate the over-deletion rate empirically (how many triples with multiple derivations exist in the 2M store, and how many would be over-deleted); ideally store derivation-set IDs so merged blocks stay distinguishable.

W4 — The confidence score is used for thresholding but never characterized (§4.4). The 0.4 emit threshold and the 0.05 floor gate everything written to the store, yet calibration is explicitly unmeasured, and §5.3/B.2 shows v7's emission volume collapsed when the corpus changed — i.e., the threshold's selectivity is corpus-dependent. Fix: one reliability diagram or a simple precision-vs-confidence bin table on held-out predictions; it costs little and makes the threshold defensible.

W5 — Model case study (§5, Appendix B) is long and weakly connected to the claim. Since the machinery is generator-independent (demonstrated well in §6.5), the v3–v10 debugging history occupies roughly a quarter of the paper for a model the paper itself declares "weak." Fix: cut §5.2–5.4 and Appendix B to a compact table; move the narratives to the repository. Use the space for W1/W3 experiments.

W6 — Single-machine, single-author, synthetic-dominated evaluation of the core operation (§6.1–6.2). Correctness is against synthetic graphs plus real stores with only two generated hops; real chains are shallow and the 2M-store inference covered 3,000 subjects. Fix: construct longer chains (e.g., 5-pass inference) at least once on the 153k store, and report variance across machines or at least state the hardware precisely.

(4) Overstated / unsupported / inconsistent claims
Abstract vs §3.1: "the pipeline's own outputs never re-enter a training corpus" is stated absolutely; §3.1 shows it holds only for outputs written by Loka's own pipeline with the flag. (W2.)
§6.2, "matched an independent closure on all 8,621 required removals" (also abstract): the 8,621 figure counts (entity, generated-triple) pairs, not distinct removals (§6.2 defines it that way). The abstract phrasing invites misreading it as 8,621 triples.
§6.5, "by this result, a generator changes what is predicted, not what the record costs": this is established for exactly two generators, one of which is non-learned. Given the abstract's framing ("our claims concern the provenance machinery"), one retrieval-based generator (the interactive path of §7.2 is conveniently excluded) would be needed to support the generality.
§6.3, encoding comparison: the named-graph variant is "counted but not queried" — fine, and disclosed — but the section title ("Encoding cost against reification and named graphs") implies a symmetric comparison that was not run. The §6.3 admission that the reified join is faster on the citation query is commendably honest; make sure the abstract doesn't quietly rely on the "2.8× fewer rows" framing without the query-speed caveat.
Appendix A perplexities: v11–v14 perplexity rises as corpora grow (279 → 202), and perplexity is declared non-comparable across corpora (§5.1). Yet §5.3 and B.2 use cross-version behavioural trends partly attributed to training length/corpus. The v7 64% catalog-share anomaly (9 of 14 emissions) is admitted as unexplained — with n=14 that cell is nearly meaningless and should not appear as a trend point.
§6.2 timing tables: two tables report retract_set on the same graphs differing by 15–20% (86.3 vs 71.5 ms), explained as session variance. Fine, but then the abstract's "about 0.1 s" is the slower of two measurements of the same quantity; the abstract rounds 85 ms up, which is defensible but slightly odd — state "about 0.1 s (70–86 ms across sessions)."
Internally consistent (checked): 263+93=356 generated triples (§6.2); 28,448−8,762=19,686 and 6,090+13,596=19,686 (§6.4); 333/937=2.8× and 125,570/82,839=1.5× (§6.3); 105 = 23+82 (§4.4); the SPARQL ratios 10.0/8.8/6.6/6.0× all recompute correctly. The paper is unusually arithmetically clean.
(5) Minor issues
Terminology churn (§3.1): propositionInferredFrom → propositionSelectedFrom renamed "shortly before submission," with evaluated stores still under the old IRI. For a paper arguing for durable provenance, this is ironic; consider an explicit alias/version mechanism and say so.
§4.3: the role set is typeset {SPECIAL, S, P, 0} and the separator as [SEP_0] — presumably O/[SEP_O]; same typo in the tokenization template on p.8.
§2.1 introduces «s p o» notation but the rest of the paper uses <<...>>; pick one.

You are a critical peer reviewer for a systems/databases venue. Review the attached paper, which is about to be submitted to arXiv (cs.DB). Give: (1) a one-paragraph summary; (2) a recommendation (Strong Accept / Accept / Weak Accept / Weak Reject / Reject); (3) the main weaknesses, each with the section it concerns and a concrete fix; (4) any claims that are overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent with the paper's own tables; (5) minor issues (clarity, terminology, citations). 6:51pm
Thought for 7s
Review: "Loka: Provenance for Retracting Model-Generated Triples in an RDF-star Store"
(1) Summary

The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that stores model-generated triples alongside curated ones, annotated in a reserved namespace (propositionGenerated, propositionGeneratedBy, propositionConfidence, propositionSelectedFrom) with quoted-triple pointers to the statements the prediction procedure consumed ("selection provenance"). Because dependencies are explicit graph edges, the store supports node-rooted cascade retraction, and three pipeline guards keep generated triples and system metadata out of training corpora. The loop is exercised end-to-end with a series of from-scratch transformers (v3–v14) on label-substituted Wikidata. Retraction is validated against an independent reference on synthetic graphs (up to 5M rows) and on real 153k and 2M-triple stores; it is 6–10× faster than an equivalent SPARQL-star closure. The authors are candid that the model itself is weak — below a predicate-frequency baseline — and scope their claims to the provenance machinery.

(2) Recommendation: Weak Accept

The problem is real and timely, the mechanism is concrete and tested against an independent reference (which found a genuine defect, a good sign of honest evaluation), and the artifact release is exemplary. But the evaluation is thin in places the claims depend on (scaling, calibration, third-party writers), and the case-study model adds 5 pages of debugging narrative whose contribution to the core claim is limited. A systems venue should value the operational provenance/retraction design, but the paper overreaches in a few places detailed below.

(3) Main weaknesses (with fixes)

W1 — Scaling claim rests on two points (§6.2). The conclusion states cost "follows the size of the removal rather than of the store," but the paper itself concedes this is "two data points," and the 100k store removes more triples (120,461) than the 1M store (106,255), so the confound is not even controlled. The per-triple cost also varies 0.31–0.8 µs unexplained. Fix: run a proper 2-D grid — store size × removal size (e.g., 4 store sizes × 4 root choices with known removal-set sizes) and report a fit; even 20 cells on a laptop would settle it.

W2 — The corpus-exclusion invariant is enforced in the pipeline, not the store (§3.1). The abstract's "the pipeline's own outputs never re-enter a training corpus" is unconditional, but §3.1 admits the store accepts any triple via POST /triples, so a generated triple written by any other tool without the flag silently enters the next corpus. For a store paper this is the central invariant, and it is guaranteed only by convention. Fix: either add a store-level mode requiring generated flags on (or provenance blocks for) writes from designated "generated" writers, or state the trust model explicitly in the abstract and §3.1.

W3 — Statement-level retraction is incompleteness papered over by node-granularity (§3.4, §7.2). Citing one statement per contributing neighbour means a single-statement deletion (or correction) would miss dependencies; the "merged citations over-delete" issue (§7.2) is a real correctness gap vs. counting derivations (Gupta et al., 1993). Both are acknowledged but left as limitations. Fix: at minimum, evaluate the over-deletion rate empirically (how many triples with multiple derivations exist in the 2M store, and how many would be over-deleted); ideally store derivation-set IDs so merged blocks stay distinguishable.

W4 — The confidence score is used for thresholding but never characterized (§4.4). The 0.4 emit threshold and the 0.05 floor gate everything written to the store, yet calibration is explicitly unmeasured, and §5.3/B.2 shows v7's emission volume collapsed when the corpus changed — i.e., the threshold's selectivity is corpus-dependent. Fix: one reliability diagram or a simple precision-vs-confidence bin table on held-out predictions; it costs little and makes the threshold defensible.

W5 — Model case study (§5, Appendix B) is long and weakly connected to the claim. Since the machinery is generator-independent (demonstrated well in §6.5), the v3–v10 debugging history occupies roughly a quarter of the paper for a model the paper itself declares "weak." Fix: cut §5.2–5.4 and Appendix B to a compact table; move the narratives to the repository. Use the space for W1/W3 experiments.

W6 — Single-machine, single-author, synthetic-dominated evaluation of the core operation (§6.1–6.2). Correctness is against synthetic graphs plus real stores with only two generated hops; real chains are shallow and the 2M-store inference covered 3,000 subjects. Fix: construct longer chains (e.g., 5-pass inference) at least once on the 153k store, and report variance across machines or at least state the hardware precisely.

(4) Overstated / unsupported / inconsistent claims
Abstract vs §3.1: "the pipeline's own outputs never re-enter a training corpus" is stated absolutely; §3.1 shows it holds only for outputs written by Loka's own pipeline with the flag. (W2.)
§6.2, "matched an independent closure on all 8,621 required removals" (also abstract): the 8,621 figure counts (entity, generated-triple) pairs, not distinct removals (§6.2 defines it that way). The abstract phrasing invites misreading it as 8,621 triples.
§6.5, "by this result, a generator changes what is predicted, not what the record costs": this is established for exactly two generators, one of which is non-learned. Given the abstract's framing ("our claims concern the provenance machinery"), one retrieval-based generator (the interactive path of §7.2 is conveniently excluded) would be needed to support the generality.
§6.3, encoding comparison: the named-graph variant is "counted but not queried" — fine, and disclosed — but the section title ("Encoding cost against reification and named graphs") implies a symmetric comparison that was not run. The §6.3 admission that the reified join is faster on the citation query is commendably honest; make sure the abstract doesn't quietly rely on the "2.8× fewer rows" framing without the query-speed caveat.
Appendix A perplexities: v11–v14 perplexity rises as corpora grow (279 → 202), and perplexity is declared non-comparable across corpora (§5.1). Yet §5.3 and B.2 use cross-version behavioural trends partly attributed to training length/corpus. The v7 64% catalog-share anomaly (9 of 14 emissions) is admitted as unexplained — with n=14 that cell is nearly meaningless and should not appear as a trend point.
§6.2 timing tables: two tables report retract_set on the same graphs differing by 15–20% (86.3 vs 71.5 ms), explained as session variance. Fine, but then the abstract's "about 0.1 s" is the slower of two measurements of the same quantity; the abstract rounds 85 ms up, which is defensible but slightly odd — state "about 0.1 s (70–86 ms across sessions)."

(5) Minor issues

§4.3: the role set is typeset {SPECIAL, S, P, 0} and the separator as [SEP_0] — presumably O/[SEP_O]; same typo in the tokenization template on p.8.

content.text:
Your sense is right, and it explains what the reviewers are reacting to.

**Why training comes up at all.** The paper still carries Loka's original idea, from when this was a model-training project:
1. a model trained on the store's triples writes new triples back into the store;
2. the next model gets trained on that store;
3. so without a guard, a model ends up trained on its predecessor's guesses.

The reserved namespace and the "generated" flag were built to stop that, and the paper still lists it as **Contribution 1**. The abstract also says the pipeline's outputs "never re-enter a training corpus". The reviewers are taking the paper at its word.

Claude made the sharpest point: v11–v14 were trained straight from the Wikidata dump, not from a Loka store, so that loop was never actually closed. The training-exclusion claim is a leftover from the earlier phase, as you suspected. The same goes for the model sections (§5 and Appendix B, the v3–v14 debugging history), which Claude and Mistral both called too long for a databases paper.

If this is really a provenance/ontology paper (generated facts carry a record of which stored facts they came from, and retraction follows that record), then the fix is not more wording about training. It's to **demote or remove training exclusion as a contribution and shrink the model material.** The model would then just be the thing that produces the triples, and any generator would do; §6.5 already shows a dumb frequency counter gives the same provenance. That's a restructuring decision, so it's yours.

**Jena.** The paper says any RDF-star database could compute the same retraction with ordinary queries. We only tested that on Loka itself, and running the same queries on Jena would back it up. It's optional; the paper could also just say "in principle".

**Retraction cost vs store size.** The claim is that deleting 100k dependent triples takes about as long in a 5M-row store as in a 0.5M-row one: the work scales with what gets removed, not with how much is stored. Lean fits this well, with one honest caveat:
- **What Lean can prove:** the algorithm does a bounded number of index lookups per removed triple, so the lookup count depends only on the size of the removal.
- **What it can't remove:** each lookup in a sorted index still costs a little more in a bigger store (logarithmically). The exact statement is "cost ∝ removed × log(store size)".

content.text:
Your sense is right, and it explains what the reviewers are reacting to.

**Why training comes up at all.** The paper still carries Loka's original idea, from when this was a model-training project:
1. a model trained on the store's triples writes new triples back into the store;
2. the next model gets trained on that store;
3. so without a guard, a model ends up trained on its predecessor's guesses.

The reserved namespace and the "generated" flag were built to stop that, and the paper still lists it as **Contribution 1**. The abstract also says the pipeline's outputs "never re-enter a training corpus". The reviewers are taking the paper at its word.

Claude made the sharpest point: v11–v14 were trained straight from the Wikidata dump, not from a Loka store, so that loop was never actually closed. The training-exclusion claim is a leftover from the earlier phase, as you suspected. The same goes for the model sections (§5 and Appendix B, the v3–v14 debugging history), which Claude and Mistral both called too long for a databases paper.

If this is really a provenance/ontology paper (generated facts carry a record of which stored facts they came from, and retraction follows that record), then the fix is not more wording about training. It's to **demote or remove training exclusion as a contribution and shrink the model material.** The model would then just be the thing that produces the triples, and any generator would do; §6.5 already shows a dumb frequency counter gives the same provenance. That's a restructuring decision, so it's yours.

**Jena.** The paper says any RDF-star database could compute the same retraction with ordinary queries. We only tested that on Loka itself, and running the same queries on Jena would back it up. It's optional; the paper could also just say "in principle".

**Retraction cost vs store size.** The claim is that deleting 100k dependent triples takes about as long in a 5M-row store as in a 0.5M-row one: the work scales with what gets removed, not with how much is stored. Lean fits this well, with one honest caveat:
- **What Lean can prove:** the algorithm does a bounded number of index lookups per removed triple, so the lookup count depends only on the size of the removal.
- **What it can't remove:** each lookup in a sorted index still costs a little more in a bigger store (logarithmically). The exact statement is "cost ∝ removed × log(store size)".

That proof would replace the "two data points" weakness with a theorem, which is stronger than more benchmarks.

**What I'm doing now:**
- I'm holding the two queued wording fixes about training exclusion and the provenance-vs-training distinction (queue items 2 and 3), so the cron doesn't polish text you may cut. The other queued fixes are neutral and can go ahead.
- I'm running Qwen with 1996 as the birth year, since you've given it.

# Loka: Provenance for Retracting Model-Generated Triples in an RDF-star Store

**Code:** <https://github.com/EmmaLeonhart/Loka> (release `v0.4.7`: <https://github.com/EmmaLeonhart/Loka/releases/tag/v0.4.7>) · **Model checkpoints:** <https://huggingface.co/datasets/EmmaLeonhart/loka> (`checkpoints/wikidata_v3.pt`–`wikidata_v14.pt`, plus per-epoch checkpoints for v13 and v14, snapshot tags `v13.*` `v14.*`) · **Normalized-Wikidata training corpora (v11+):** <https://huggingface.co/datasets/EmmaLeonhart/normalized-wikidata> (snapshot tags `v11-50k`, `v12-100k`, `v13-500k`, `v14-1M`) · **Source dataset:** <https://huggingface.co/datasets/philippesaade/wikidata>

---

## Abstract

Once model-generated statements are written into a knowledge graph next to curated data, it is hard to tell them apart, to keep them out of the next model's training data, or to remove them when a statement they depended on turns out to be wrong. We describe Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that stores model-predicted triples alongside curated ones and annotates each with RDF-star statements in a reserved namespace: the generating model, a confidence, and quoted pointers to the stored statements the prediction procedure took as input, which we call selection provenance. The namespace is checked at corpus extraction, at candidate selection and when the inference pipeline writes, and the extractor drops every triple flagged as generated, so the pipeline's own outputs never re-enter a training corpus. Because these dependencies are explicit graph edges, the store supports cascade retraction: removing a node also removes every generated triple that transitively depended on one of its statements, without following ordinary data edges. We exercise the loop with a series of small transformers trained from scratch on label-substituted Wikidata triples and use them to evaluate the provenance machinery on real data. Tested against an independent reference, retraction computes a 106k-triple removal from a 5M-row store in about 0.1 s in memory, and on a real 2M-triple Wikidata store with chained predictions it matched an independent closure on all 8,621 required removals. Selection provenance records what the procedure used, not what the model relied on, and on held-out triples the model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline: our claims concern the provenance machinery, not the model. Code, all checkpoints and the cleaned corpora are released.

---

## 1. Introduction

Knowledge graphs are increasingly extended by models: link predictors propose missing edges, and language models extract or generate statements. Once a predicted statement is stored, a typical triplestore holds it exactly like a curated one. Whatever provenance exists lives outside the graph, in pipeline logs or a separate metadata table. Three problems follow. A query cannot ask which answers came from a model. A model's output can flow into the training corpus of the next model. And when a source statement is found to be wrong, nothing in the store says which generated statements were derived from it.

RDF-star lets a triple be the subject of other triples. Loka uses this to keep provenance in the same graph as the data it describes. Every model-predicted triple is written together with RDF-star annotations, in a reserved namespace, recording that it was generated, by which model, with what confidence, and from which stored statements. These annotations can be queried with ordinary SPARQL-star, used to exclude generated statements from training corpora, and followed to retract everything that depended on a withdrawn statement.

We are specific about what the dependency edge means. In our prediction procedure, a candidate (subject, predicate) pair is proposed from the subject's existing statements and those of its graph neighbours, and the model then predicts an object from the subject and predicate labels alone. The `propositionSelectedFrom` edges record exactly the subject's statements whose match with a neighbour led to the proposal, plus one statement of each such neighbour. We call this *selection provenance*. It is a record of the procedure's inputs, which is what retraction needs; it is not evidence that the cited statements support the prediction, and not a record of what the model attended to.

### Contributions

1. **A reserved provenance namespace with three-layer exclusion.** Predicates under `http://loka.dev/provenance/` are system-only. The corpus extractor drops every triple flagged generated and every reserved-namespace row, so neither generated statements nor their annotations enter a training corpus; the candidate selector and the writer also refuse reserved predicates independently, so the model can neither learn nor emit system metadata even if one of those guards regresses. (§3.1)

2. **An RDF-star annotation schema for generated triples.** Each generated triple carries a fixed block of annotations on the quoted triple: a generated flag, the model version, a confidence, and selection-provenance edges whose objects are themselves quoted triples: the stored statements that led the procedure to propose the (subject, predicate) slot. They record the candidate's proposal, not a justification of the predicted object, which the model produces from the subject and predicate labels. (§3.2)

3. **Cascade retraction.** Removing a node removes its statements and every generated triple that transitively depended on them. Traversal follows only selection-provenance edges and stays inside the reserved namespace, so ordinary data edges are never treated as dependencies. We test it against an independent reference implementation and measure its cost. (§3.4, §6.1–6.2)

4. **A case study on Wikidata.** A from-scratch masked-triple transformer series (v3–v14, all checkpoints and corpora released) exercises the loop end to end on real data. (§5)

---

## 2. Background and related work

### 2.1 RDF-star

RDF-star extends RDF so that a triple can appear, *quoted*, as the subject or object of another triple (Hartig, 2017; W3C RDF-star Community Group). The notation `<<s p o>>` denotes the triple s p o as a term, without asserting it. This admits direct annotation of statements:

```
:Tokyo :population "13929286" .
<<:Tokyo :population "13929286">> :measuredAt "2020-01-01" .
<<:Tokyo :population "13929286">> :statedIn :census2020 .
```

Wikidata expresses the same information through reified statement nodes carrying qualifiers and references (Vrandečić and Krötzsch, 2014); RDF-star collapses them into one structural primitive. Loka interns a quoted triple to a content-addressed identifier, `quoted_triple_id(s, p, o)`, a hash of the three component ids, and keeps a reverse index from that identifier to (s, p, o) so that a quoted triple can be rendered and dereferenced.

### 2.2 Provenance

Recording where statements come from is an old concern of the Semantic Web. Named graphs attach provenance and trust information to sets of triples (Carroll et al., 2005), and the W3C PROV-O ontology gives a vocabulary for entities, activities and agents and their derivation relations (Lebo et al., 2013). Nanopublications package a single assertion with its provenance and publication information as a set of named graphs (Groth et al., 2010). Inside a triplestore, TripleProv stores provenance next to the data and answers lineage queries natively (Wylot et al., 2014). In database theory, provenance has been formalised as *why-provenance*, the source tuples that witness an output, and *where-provenance*, the locations a value was copied from (Buneman et al., 2001), and generalised by provenance semirings, which annotate query results with polynomials over source annotations (Green et al., 2007). Selection provenance borrows the shape of why-provenance, one set of source statements per output, but not its meaning. A why-provenance witness is a set of source tuples from which the output follows; the statements we record are the ones that led the procedure to propose the (subject, predicate) slot, and the object value comes from the model, not from them. It is provenance of the proposal, not a witness for the value. All of these record provenance; none of the RDF ones defines how a store should act on it when a source is withdrawn. Most operate at the granularity of a graph or an explicit provenance resource. We use RDF-star to attach provenance to individual triples directly, with a small fixed vocabulary for one case, model-generated statements; mapping it onto PROV-O is left to consumers, and `prov:used` on the generating activity fits `propositionSelectedFrom` better than `prov:wasDerivedFrom`, which would claim the value was derived from the cited statements. What we add is not a provenance vocabulary but an operational use of it inside the store: exclusion from training corpora and cascade retraction.

### 2.3 Knowledge-graph completion

Link prediction scores candidate completions of (subject, predicate, ?) queries. Embedding models such as TransE (Bordes et al., 2013) and RotatE (Sun et al., 2019) learn entity and relation vectors; transformer-based models score triples as text (KG-BERT; Yao et al., 2019) or generate the missing entity as a sequence (KGT5; Saxena et al., 2022). The standard evaluation reports mean reciprocal rank and Hits@k in the filtered setting, which removes other known true answers before ranking (Bordes et al., 2013); we follow it, with the tie-aware rank of Berrendorf et al. (2020), and use PyKEEN (Ali et al., 2021) for the TransE baseline. These systems output scores or ranked candidates. Writing the chosen completions back into

1. One-Paragraph Summary
This paper introduces Loka, an RDF-star triplestore designed to manage model-generated knowledge graph statements alongside curated data. Loka annotates generated triples with a reserved provenance namespace that records the generating model, a confidence score, and "selection provenance"—the specific stored statements that led the inference procedure to propose the subject-predicate pair. This design enables two key features: (1) strict exclusion of generated triples and their metadata from subsequent training corpora to prevent data leakage, and (2) cascade retraction, which efficiently removes generated triples that transitively depend on a retracted source statement. The authors evaluate the system using a series of custom-trained transformers on Wikidata, demonstrating that retraction is both correct (validated against an independent reference) and highly efficient (e.g., ~85 ms for a 106k-triple removal in a 5M-row store), while also showing that the RDF-star annotation schema is significantly more compact than standard reification or named graphs.
2. Recommendation
Weak Accept
The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem (provenance and retraction of LLM/KGE outputs in knowledge graphs) with a well-engineered, transparent solution. The authors are commendably honest about the limitations of their generative model and the scope of their evaluation. However, the reliance on node-level (rather than statement-level) retraction and the use of a very weak generative baseline limit the immediate practical impact for a top-tier databases venue. Addressing the profiling gaps and clarifying a few terminological choices would strengthen the submission significantly.
3. Main Weaknesses
W1: Node-level retraction limits practical utility in real-world KGs.
Section: 3.4, 7.2
Issue: The paper explicitly states that retraction is "node-rooted," meaning retracting a single false statement removes the entire entity node and all generated triples about it. In real-world KGs, users frequently need to retract a single erroneous statement (e.g., a hallucinated birth date) without deleting the entire entity or its other valid generated statements. The paper dismisses statement-level retraction due to "citation explosion" (median 105 citations vs. 9), but this is a fundamental limitation for a database system.
Concrete Fix: Implement or formally evaluate a bounded statement-level retraction mechanism (e.g., capping citations per prediction at a fixed number, similar to the bounded selector) and analyze the trade-off between citation completeness and retraction accuracy. Alternatively, provide a clear workaround pattern (e.g., reifying the specific statement into a blank node for targeted retraction).
W2: Weak generative baseline limits validation of the provenance machinery.
Section: 6.4, 6.5, 7.1
Issue: The authors correctly state that their claims concern the provenance machinery, not the model. However, the utility of this machinery is inherently tied to the behavior of the generator. The evaluated model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline, and the fallback evaluation in §6.5 uses that same trivial frequency baseline. This fails to demonstrate how the system handles the complex, plausible, but incorrect generations typical of modern KGEs or LLMs, which is the primary use case for cascade retraction.
Concrete Fix: Include an evaluation using a standard, stronger knowledge graph completion model (e.g., RotatE via PyKEEN, or a small fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence model like Flan-T5) to prove that the provenance recording and retraction machinery scales and functions identically with realistic, high-quality generators.
W3: Unisolated performance variance in retraction cost.
Section: 6.2
Issue: The authors note a 1.6× run-to-run variation in absolute times and admit, "we have not isolated which factor accounts for the difference" in per-triple cost between small and large graphs. For a systems/database venue, leaving performance variance unprofiled weakens the claim that cost strictly follows the size of the removal set.
Concrete Fix: Add a brief performance breakdown (e.g., percentage of time spent in reverse-index dereferencing, hash-map lookups, and memory allocation) to explain the variance and solidify the scaling claims.
4. Overstated, Unsupported, or Inconsistent Claims
Overstated scaling claim: The Abstract and Conclusion state that retraction cost "follows the size of the removal rather than of the store." While the data is suggestive, Section 6.2 explicitly admits this is based on only "two data points" (the 0.5M and 5M-row stores). This should be softened to "preliminary evidence suggests" or "is consistent with scaling based on removal size rather than store size."
Inaccurate phrasing regarding previews: In Section 6.2, the text states: "Over HTTP the preview took a median of 1.4 ms... and removed a median of 83 triples." A preview operation identifies candidates for removal; it does not remove them. This should be corrected to "identified a median of 83 triples for removal."
Misleading probability description: In Section 4.4, the paper states: "The penalty divides probabilities... p is not renormalised afterwards." If probabilities are divided and not renormalized, they no longer sum to 1, meaning p is no longer a valid probability distribution. While this may be intentional for a greedy decoding floor check, it should be explicitly clarified (e.g., "we treat the resulting scores as relative confidence weights for thresholding, not as a normalized probability distribution").
5. Minor Issues (Clarity, Terminology, Citations)
Terminology / Namespace collision (Section 3.2): The paper states, "prov: abbreviates the reserved namespace." The reserved namespace is http://loka.dev/provenance/. Using the prefix prov: is highly discouraged, as it is the universally registered prefix for the W3C PROV-O ontology (http://www.w3.org/ns/prov#). This will cause confusion and potential interoperability issues. The authors should use a distinct prefix, such as lokaprov: or loka:.
Clarity in security guarantees (Section 3.1): The paragraph explaining the three layers of enforcement is convoluted: "The guards for that second invariant overlap only on the output side: the selector or the emit-time guard alone stops a reserved predicate being proposed or written, while keeping annotation rows out of training rests on the extractor's prefix filter alone." This should be rewritten as a clear bulleted list mapping each invariant (e.g., "Prevent model from seeing metadata," "Prevent model from emitting metadata") to the specific guard(s) that enforce it.
Citation missing year (References): The reference "W3C RDF-star Community Group. RDF-star and SPARQL-star. Final Community Group Report." is missing a publication year. (It should be 2023).
Baseline caveat (Section 6.2): The paper notes that the SPARQL-star baseline is 6–10× slower partly because "the engine does not evaluate a property path whose end is a quoted pattern," requiring a workaround. This should be explicitly framed as a limitation of the current query executor's implementation rather than an inherent performance flaw of SPARQL-star itself, to ensure the 6–10× speedup claim is interpreted correctly.

## Abstract

Once model-generated statements are written into a knowledge graph next to curated data, it is hard to tell them apart, to keep them out of the next model's training data, or to remove them when a statement they depended on turns out to be wrong. Selection provenance records what the procedure used, not what the model relied on, and on held-out triples the model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline: our claims concern the provenance machinery, not the model. Knowledge graphs are increasingly extended by models: link predictors propose missing edges, and language models extract or generate statements. Three problems follow. A query cannot ask which answers came from a model. A model's output can flow into the training corpus of the next model. And when a source statement is found to be wrong, nothing in the store says which generated statements were derived from it.

It is a record of the procedure's inputs, which is what retraction needs; it is not evidence that the cited statements support the prediction, and not a record of what the model attended to.

lines: Committing a retraction also deletes the set from the persistent (sled) store and flushes it before replying. We committed retractions of 30 randomly chosen entities in turn on a copy of a store. With one storage transaction per removed triple, as the engine first did, the unbounded-selector store took a median of 140 ms per commit and up to 30 s (1.28 ms per removed triple; 43,085 rows removed in all); removing the whole set in a single transaction brought the same 30 commits to a median of 8.3 ms and a maximum of 0.31 s (0.06 ms per removed triple). On the bounded-selector store above, the 30 commits removed 6,380 rows, at a median of 4.6 ms and a maximum of 31 ms. Every restart reloaded exactly the expected number of rows.

-At larger scale, we imported 2,000,623 real triples (8,806 entities with every claim, label, qualifier and reference) from the same Wikidata dump into a fresh store, ran both inference passes over 3,000 subjects sampled with a fixed seed, and repeated the checks. The passes produced 526 and 146 predictions, 100 of the second citing a first-pass prediction (672 generated triples, 13,318 annotation rows; a median of 17 citations each, maximum 39). Over 8,621 required removals across 2,667 entities, the retraction preview matched the independent closure exactly, with nothing missed and nothing extra; it took a median of 2.3 ms (p95 6.2 ms) and removed a median of 140 triples (maximum 20,600). Thirty committed retractions removed 5,377 rows at a median of 24 ms (maximum 43 ms), and a restart reloaded exactly the expected 2,009,885 rows. Inference itself was the slow step at this scale: about 5 s per subject on CPU, against about 1 s on the 153k-triple graph.

lines: -Once model-generated statements are written into a knowledge graph next to curated data, it is hard to tell them apart, to keep them out of the next model's training data, or to remove them when a statement they depended on turns out to be wrong. We describe Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that stores model-predicted triples alongside curated ones and annotates each with RDF-star statements in a reserved namespace: the generating model, a confidence, and quoted pointers to the stored statements the prediction procedure took as input, which we call selection provenance. The namespace is checked at corpus extraction, at candidate selection and when the inference pipeline writes, and the extractor drops every triple flagged as generated, so the pipeline's own outputs never re-enter a training corpus. Because these dependencies are explicit graph edges, the store supports cascade retraction: removing a node also removes every generated triple that transitively depended on one of its statements, without following ordinary data edges. We exercise the loop with a series of small transformers trained from scratch on label-substituted Wikidata triples and use them to evaluate the provenance machinery on real data. Tested against an independent reference, retraction computes a 106k-triple removal from a 5M-row store in about 0.1 s in memory, and on a real 2M-triple Wikidata store with chained predictions it matched an independent closure on all 8,621 required removals. Selection provenance records what the procedure used, not what the model relied on, and on held-out triples the model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline: our claims concern the provenance machinery, not the model. Code, all checkpoints and the cleaned corpora are released.

+Once model-generated statements are written into a knowledge graph next to curated data, it is hard to tell them apart, to keep them out of the next model's training data, or to remove them when a statement they depended on turns out to be wrong. We describe Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that stores model-predicted triples alongside curated ones and annotates each with RDF-star statements in a reserved namespace: the generating model, a confidence, and quoted pointers to the stored statements the prediction procedure took as input, which we call selection provenance. The namespace is checked at corpus extraction, at candidate selection and when the inference pipeline writes, and the extractor drops every triple flagged as generated, so the pipeline's own outputs never re-enter a training corpus. Because these dependencies are explicit graph edges, the store supports cascade retraction: removing a node also removes every generated triple that transitively depended on one of its statements, without following ordinary data edges. We exercise the loop with a series of small transformers trained from scratch on label-substituted Wikidata triples and use them to evaluate the provenance machinery on real data. Retraction agrees with an independent reference implementation on generated graphs, computes the set for a 106k-triple removal from a 5M-row store in about 85 ms in memory (deleting it from disk is measured separately), and on a real 2M-triple Wikidata store with chained predictions it matched an independently computed closure on all 8,621 required removals, counted as (entity, generated triple) pairs. Selection provenance records what the procedure used, not what the model relied on, and on held-out triples the model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline: our claims concern the provenance machinery, not the model. Code, all checkpoints and the cleaned corpora are released.

The query-based closure is 6–10× slower and, like `retract_set`, takes about the same time on the 0.5M-row and 5M-row stores. The dedicated traversal is therefore an optimisation, not a requirement: any SPARQL-star store that holds the annotation block can compute the same retraction set with standard queries. The `retract_set` times in this table are about 15–20 % below those in the table above, which was measured by a separate benchmark binary minutes earlier; this is the run-to-run variation in absolute times noted above, and the ratio within one process is the comparable figure. Raw output is under `paper/supplementary/retract-baseline/`, and the benchmark is `loka-sparql/benches/retract_baseline.rs`.
## Standing constraints

- After any paper change: Paper PDF CI green, then refresh `pages/arxiv/` (PDF, source tarball,
  and the abstract copies in `pages/arxiv/index.html` and `paper/arxiv/METADATA.md`).
- Thermal limits on this laptop: never run `loka serve` + ingest + training together; no
  multi-hour experiment re-runs without asking Emma. v14 training is donor-only.
- Numbers in the paper are only changed when recomputed from the paper's tables or re-measured.
- Open decision for Emma (TODO.md): whether retraction should also sweep curated annotations
  of a removed triple; the paper documents current behaviour (§3.4, §7.2).
- LLM reviews (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Mistral, Gemini) are run in Chrome on the `/arxiv/` PDF
  with the prompt saved in `paper/reviews/llm-round-2026-10-29.md`. A "permission denied" from
  the extension can be transient: retry before reporting a reviewer as unavailable (Emma,
  2026-10-29). clawRxiv has given no reviews since 2026-10-16 (site-wide).
- When Emma is angry, freeze and answer from context; do not search or start anything new.

The store then held real dependency chains of two generated hops (356 generated triples, 4,817 annotation rows). For each of the 983 entities we called the server's retraction preview and compared it with an independently computed closure: a generated triple must be removed if it touches the entity, cites a statement touching the entity, or cites a removed generated triple. content.content:
We compare the annotation block with the two standard ways of attaching provenance to individual statements in plain RDF, using real data. We pulled a breadth-first Wikidata neighbourhood of `Q42` (14,819 triples, 169 entities), loaded it, and ran the v13 model's inference over every subject, which wrote 38 generated triples with 181 selection-provenance edges (113 distinct cited statements). The same generated set was then re-encoded (a) as standard RDF reification with PROV-O, where each generated triple gets an `rdf:Statement` node carrying the metadata and `prov:wasDerivedFrom` links to `rdf:Statement` nodes for the cited statements, and (b) as one named graph per generated triple, with the cited statements still reified so they can be pointed at.

| Encoding | Rows | Bytes (N-Triples / N-Quads) |
|---|---|---|
| RDF-star annotation block (ours) | **333** | **82,839** |
| Reification + PROV-O | 937 | 125,570 |
| Named graph per prediction | 785 quads | 106,767 |

In rows the RDF-star block is 2.8× smaller than reification and 2.4× smaller than named graphs; in bytes the gaps are 1.5× and 1.3×, because the extra rows are short. Most of the difference is the cost of making a curated statement citable: RDF-star quotes it in place, while the other encodings need four extra rows per cited statement.

We also asked both triple-based stores the same question for each of the 169 entities X, "which generated triples cite a statement whose object is X?" (a nested SPARQL-star pattern on one side, a five-pattern join over reification nodes on the other). Both returned identical answers for all 169 entities, with the stores reloaded from disk. Median latency over HTTP was 0.66 ms for the RDF-star query and 0.56 ms for the reified join (p95 1.08 and 0.97 ms). An earlier executor took 5.14 ms on the RDF-star query, because it found quoted subjects by hashing every stored triple; it now walks the rows of the bound annotation predicate and dereferences each quoted subject through the reverse index (§2.1). The RDF-star encoding needs 2.8 times fewer rows (1.5 times fewer bytes) than reification, but on this query the reified join was about 0.1 ms faster: the advantage shown here is in storage, not query speed. Loka has no named-graph support, so (b) was counted but not queried, and the comparison with it is of rows and bytes only.

### 6.4 Link prediction

7	## Abstract
8	
9	Once model-generated statements are written into a knowledge graph next to curated data, it is hard to tell them apart, to keep them out of the next model's training data, or to remove them when a statement they depended on turns out to be wrong. We describe Loka, an RDF-star triplestore that stores model-predicted triples alongside curated ones and annotates each with RDF-star statements in a reserved namespace: the generating model, a confidence, and quoted pointers to the stored statements the prediction procedure took as input, which we call selection provenance. The namespace is checked at corpus extraction, at candidate selection and when the inference pipeline writes, and the extractor drops every triple flagged as generated, so the pipeline's own outputs never re-enter a training corpus. Because these dependencies are explicit graph edges, the store supports cascade retraction: removing a node also removes every generated triple that transitively depended on one of its statements, without following ordinary data edges. We exercise the loop with a series of small transformers trained from scratch on label-substituted Wikidata triples and use them to evaluate the provenance machinery on real data. Retraction agrees with an independent reference implementation on generated graphs, computes the set for a 106k-triple removal from a 5M-row store in about 85 ms in memory (deleting it from disk is measured separately), and on a real 2M-triple Wikidata store with chained predictions it matched an independently computed closure on all 8,621 required removals, counted as (entity, generated triple) pairs. Selection provenance records what the procedure used, not what the model relied on, and on held-out triples the model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline: our claims concern the provenance machinery, not the model. Code, all checkpoints and the cleaned corpora are released.
10	
11	---
12	
13	## 1. Introduction
14	
15	Knowledge graphs are increasingly extended by models: link predictors propose missing edges, and language models extract or generate statements. Once a predicted statement is stored, a typical triplestore holds it exactly like a curated one. Whatever provenance exists lives outside the graph, in pipeline logs or a separate metadata table. Three problems follow. A query cannot ask which answers came from a model. A model's output can flow into the training corpus of the next model. And when a source statement is found to be wrong, nothing in the store says which generated statements were derived from it.
16	
17	RDF-star lets a triple be the subject of other triples. Loka uses this to keep provenance in the same graph as the data it describes. Every model-predicted triple is written together with RDF-star annotations, in a reserved namespace, recording that it was generated, by which model, with what confidence, and from which stored statements. These annotations can be queried with ordinary SPARQL-star, used to exclude generated statements from training corpora, and followed to retract everything that depended on a withdrawn statement.
18	
19	We are specific about what the dependency edge means. In our prediction procedure, a candidate (subject, predicate) pair is proposed from the subject's existing statements and those of its graph neighbours, and the model then predicts an object from the subject and predicate labels alone. The `propositionSelectedFrom` edges record exactly the subject's statements whose match with a neighbour led to the proposal, plus one statement of each such neighbour. We call this *selection provenance*. It is a record of the procedure's inputs, which is what retraction needs; it is not evidence that the cited statements support the prediction, and not a record of what the model attended to.
20	
21	### Contributions
22	
23	1. **A reserved provenance namespace with three-layer exclusion.** Predicates under `http://loka.dev/provenance/` are system-only. The corpus extractor drops every triple flagged generated and every reserved-namespace row, so neither generated statements nor their annotations enter a training corpus; the candidate selector and the writer also refuse reserved predicates independently, so the model can neither learn nor emit system metadata even if one of those guards regresses. (§3.1)
24	
25	2. **An RDF-star annotation schema for generated triples.** Each generated triple carries a fixed block of annotations on the quoted triple: a generated flag, the model version, a confidence, and selection-provenance edges whose objects are themselves quoted triples: the stored statements that led the procedure to propose the (subject, predicate) slot. They record the candidate's proposal, not a justification of the predicted object, which the model produces from the subject and predicate labels. (§3.2)
26	
27	3. **Cascade retraction.** Removing a node removes its statements and every generated triple that transitively depended on them. Traversal follows only selection-provenance edges and stays inside the reserved namespace, so ordinary data edges are never treated as dependencies. We test it against an independent reference implementation and measure its cost. (§3.4, §6.1–6.2)
28	
29	4. **A case study on Wikidata.** A from-scratch masked-triple transformer series (v3–v14, all checkpoints and corpora released) exercises the loop end to end on real data. (§5)
30	
31	---

Every model-predicted triple is written together with RDF-star annotations, in a reserved namespace, recording that it was generated, by which model, with what confidence, and from which stored statements. These annotations can be queried with ordinary SPARQL-star, used to exclude generated statements from training corpora, and followed to retract everything that depended on a withdrawn statement.

We are specific about what the dependency edge means. In our prediction procedure, a candidate (subject, predicate) pair is proposed from the subject's existing statements and those of its graph neighbours, and the model then predicts an object from the subject and predicate labels alone. The `propositionSelectedFrom` edges record exactly the subject's statements whose match with a neighbour led to the proposal, plus one statement of each such neighbour. We call this *selection provenance*. It is a record of the procedure's inputs, which is what retraction needs; it is not evidence that the cited statements support the prediction, and not a record of what the model attended to.

### Contributions

1. **A reserved provenance namespace with three-layer exclusion.** Predicates under `http://loka.dev/provenance/` are system-only. The corpus extractor drops every triple flagged generated and every reserved-namespace row, so neither generated statements nor their annotations enter a training corpus; the candidate selector and the writer also refuse reserved predicates independently, so the model can neither learn nor emit system metadata even if one of those guards regresses. (§3.1)

2. **An RDF-star annotation schema for generated triples.** Each generated triple carries a fixed block of annotations on the quoted triple: a generated flag, the model version, a confidence, and selection-provenance edges whose objects are themselves quoted triples: the stored statements that led the procedure to propose the (subject, predicate) slot. They record the candidate's proposal, not a justification of the predicted object, which the model produces from the subject and predicate labels. (§3.2)

3. **Cascade retraction.** Removing a node removes its statements and every generated triple that transitively depended on them. Traversal follows only selection-provenance edges and stays inside the reserved namespace, so ordinary data edges are never treated as dependencies. We test it against an independent reference implementation and measure its cost. (§3.4, §6.1–6.2)

4. **A case study on Wikidata.** A from-scratch masked-triple transformer series (v3–v14, all checkpoints and corpora released) exercises the loop end to end on real data. (§5)

lines: **An entity-space decoder.** The engine's HNSW vector index could resolve a predicted embedding to the nearest known IRI, so that predictions are entities rather than label strings. That would make completion directly comparable with entity-ranking methods and remove BPE artifacts from stored output.

+Beyond these, the same store could serve as a harness for training models on its own graph, with the vocabulary keeping each generation's output distinguishable from the data it was trained on. We leave that open; this paper claims only the provenance record and what the store does with it.

-We described how a triplestore can hold model-generated statements next to curated ones without losing track of them: each generated triple carries RDF-star annotations, in a reserved namespace, naming its model, its confidence and the stored statements its procedure used. The case-study model is weak at completion, below a frequency baseline, which is why our claims rest on the provenance machinery rather than on the model. Code, checkpoints and corpora are released.
