content.content:
### 2.4 Attribution for generated content

Retrieval-augmented generation conditions a language model on retrieved passages (Lewis et al., 2020), and attributed question answering asks a model to return evidence supporting its answer and evaluates whether the evidence does support it (Bohnet et al., 2022). Those lines of work aim at support: the cited source should justify the output. Selection provenance makes a weaker, procedural claim: the cited statements were the input to the procedure that produced the output. That is enough for retraction, which needs to know what an output depended on, and it is not a claim of support (§7.2). Machine unlearning addresses the complementary problem of removing a training example's influence from the model itself (Bourtoule et al., 2021); cascade retraction removes a source's influence from the model's *stored outputs*, and needs no change to the model.

### 2.5 Truth maintenance and deletion propagation

Cascade retraction is closest in spirit to truth maintenance. A justification-based truth maintenance system records, for each belief, the justifications that support it and withdraws a belief when none of its justifications remains valid (Doyle, 1979). Deductive and relational databases face the same problem for materialised views: Gupta et al. (1993) give incremental algorithms that propagate deletions to derived tuples, counting alternative derivations for each derived tuple and, for recursive views, deleting an over-estimate and re-deriving. Loka's setting differs in two ways that keep the mechanism simple. Each generated triple has exactly one justification, the set of stored statements its procedure consumed, so removing any one of them removes the triple, and no alternative-derivation counting is needed. And the derived statements are not recomputable from a rule set: they are model outputs, so the dependency record must be stored at write time, which is what the RDF-star annotations do. What we contribute is not the propagation idea but its realisation inside an RDF-star store, bounded to a reserved namespace so that curated data is never treated as derived.

### 2.6 Training from scratch

The models in our case study are trained from scratch on triples, not fine-tuned from a pretrained language model. With a pretrained model, a generated triple can draw on pretraining data the store knows nothing about, so its provenance record would be incomplete by construction; training only on the corpus keeps everything the model learned inside a known, released dataset. The schema itself does not depend on this choice.

---

## 3. Architecture
105:The layers protect two different invariants. Keeping *generated triples* out of a corpus rests on the extractor's generated-flag filter alone: a generated triple uses an ordinary data predicate, so the prefix checks do not see it. Keeping *system metadata* out of the model's input and output rests on all three: the extractor's prefix filter keeps annotation rows out of training, and the selector and the emit-time guard stop the model proposing or writing a reserved predicate. The guards for that second invariant overlap only on the output side: the selector or the emit-time guard alone stops a reserved predicate being proposed or written, while keeping annotation rows out of training rests on the extractor's prefix filter alone. Each guard exists so that a regression in one path cannot silently let the model output system metadata; the selector and the emit-time guard are not covered by a test that disables the other. All of these guards sit in Loka's extractor and inference pipeline, not in the store: in keeping with storing whatever is written, the store accepts any triple over `POST /triples`, so a generated triple that another tool writes without the generated flag is not excluded from a corpus.

## 5. Case study: a model series on cleaned Wikidata

We exercised the provenance loop with a series of from-scratch models (v3–v14) trained on progressively rebuilt Wikidata corpora. Every checkpoint and corpus is released (links at the top of the paper); Appendix A lists each version's tokenizer, corpus size, training length and perplexity. The models matter here only as generators for the provenance machinery, and their completion accuracy is evaluated against baselines in §6.4. This section summarises the corpus decisions that the released models and corpora embody; Appendix B gives the examples and probe results behind them.

### 5.1 Setup

From v5 on, the architecture is fixed at the 44.5 M-parameter configuration of §4.3; from v6 on, the tokenizer is a fixed byte-level BPE vocabulary. Later versions therefore differ only in training corpus and training length. Perplexity is a training diagnostic only: it is not comparable across the word-level (v3–v5) and BPE (v6+) tokenizers, nor across corpora that differ in content as well as size.

### 5.2 Datatype leakage

The first corpus kept datatype IRIs inside literal strings, and the model trained on it (v3) learned to emit them. Stripping datatype suffixes before tokenization (§4.2) removed the pattern and *raised* perplexity (92.5 vs 53.4), because v3 had been earning cheap loss on those tokens; this is why we treat perplexity as a diagnostic, not an outcome.

### 5.3 Catalog noise

Catalog cross-reference identifiers (Wikidata's `external-id` datatype: about 80 % of properties and 75.7 % of the v6 training rows) taught v6 to emit confident identifier-shaped strings, including on unrelated predicates. From v7 on, the corpus excludes the datatypes whose values carry no transferable content, keeping 2,231 of 12,756 properties, and normalises time and quantity literals; the specification ships as `training/wikidata_excluded_predicates.json`. On a fixed behavioural probe, the share of emissions on catalog-identifier predicates fell from 40 % (v6) to 0 % (v10), though not steadily: it was 64 % at v7 (9 of only 14 emissions), which we have not explained, then 15 %, 3 % and 0 %; and a date-shaped leak onto `instance of` disappeared from v7 on (Appendix B).

### 5.4 Residual failure modes

The cleaned models still fail in narrow, consistent ways: copying the subject as the object on mostly reflexive predicates, following the most frequent predicate template, giving a value of the right type but wrong identity, and numeric-format degeneration. Appendix B shows raw examples.

### 5.5 Building the corpus without the store

Extracting training triples from the store with paged SPARQL (`LIMIT`/`OFFSET`) costs time linear in the offset, which made a 50 M-triple extraction impractical. From v11 on, the corpus is built by streaming the source parquet directly: a first pass caches English labels, a second emits one tab-separated `subject predicate object` line per kept claim, with the same exclusions and normalisations as above and with reserved-namespace triples stripped. The resulting corpora are released as a separate dataset in four sizes (Appendix A). The provenance guarantee of §3.1 is unchanged: generated triples never enter a corpus, whichever path builds it.

When a model writes statements into a knowledge graph next to curated data, the graph should say which statements came from a model, from which model, and which stored statements each was produced from, so that generated statements can be found, filtered, and removed when a statement they depended on is withdrawn. -- **Title:** Loka: Provenance for Retracting Model-Generated Triples in an RDF-star Store

-When a model writes statements into a knowledge graph next to curated data, the graph should say which statements came from a model, from which model, and which stored statements each was produced from, so that generated statements can be found, filtered, and removed when a statement they depended on is withdrawn. We describe a small provenance vocabulary for model-generated statements and its implementation in Loka, an RDF-star triplestore. Each generated triple carries RDF-star annotations in a reserved namespace: a generated flag, the generating model, a confidence, and quoted pointers to the stored statements the prediction procedure took as input, which we call selection provenance. Because these dependencies are graph edges, the store can query them with ordinary SPARQL-star, leave flagged statements out of the corpora it extracts, and retract by dependency: removing a node also removes every generated triple that transitively depended on one of its statements, without following ordinary data edges. Retraction agrees with an independent reference implementation on generated graphs, computes the set for a 106k-triple removal from a 5M-row store in about 85 ms in memory (deleting it from disk is measured separately), and on a real 2M-triple Wikidata store with chained predictions it matched an independently computed closure on all 8,621 required removals, counted as (entity, generated triple) pairs. The generated triples come from small transformers trained from scratch on Wikidata, which serve as the workload; on held-out triples they do not beat a predicate-frequency baseline. Selection provenance records what the procedure used, not what the model relied on. Code, checkpoints and corpora are released.

content.text:
The queue is empty: the review fixes and your ontology-for-AI reframe are done, and the rebuilt 17-page paper is on https://loka.emmaleonhart.com/arxiv/. Everything is committed and pushed.

**The reframe:**
- **Abstract and introduction** now lead with the provenance vocabulary and what Loka does with it: query it, filter generated triples out when it builds a corpus, and retract by dependency.
- **"Outputs never re-enter a training corpus"** is gone. That point is now a smaller Contribution 3, limited to triples Loka's own pipeline writes and flags. The model is described as the thing that produces the test data, not a contribution.
- **Training:** §2.4 and §2.6 now say that retracting a fact removes the stored outputs built on it, not what the model learned from it in training.
- **Model history:** Appendix B moved to `docs/model-history.md`, and the paper links to it.
- **World-model harness:** §8 gets one sentence leaving the "harness for training world models" idea open, without claiming it.
- **Category:** cs.AI is now primary, with cs.DB cross-listed. That was my call from your "it's an AI paper"; it's a one-line change in the metadata if you'd rather keep cs.DB.

**Review fixes:**
- §6.2 now gives the 2M store's starting row count (2,015,262), so its numbers add up.
- The abstract says "about 85 ms in memory" instead of "0.1 s", and explains what the 8,621 counts.
- §6.2 names the laptop's hardware. It also says other databases could run the plain-SPARQL version only "in principle", and doesn't run anything on Jena.
- §6.3 explains its choice of baseline encodings.
- The `prov:` prefix is now `lprov:`, since `prov:` is the prefix of an existing W3C provenance vocabulary the paper also cites.
- INTENT.md records your framing, so later runs won't suggest Jena again.

**Lean:** dropped. There's no Lean toolchain on this laptop, so it wasn't the "really easy" case you allowed.

What's left is yours: the upload at arxiv.org, then pasting me the arXiv ID.

loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Finished
2s

The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star knowledge-graph store designed to make model-generated statements identifiable, filterable, and retractable when their recorded source dependencies are removed. Its contribution is provenance infrastructure—not a better prediction model.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

What it does

Loka stores model-generated facts alongside curated facts, but adds annotations to each generated triple recording:

That it was generated.

Which model produced it.

A confidence score, which is a decoding score rather than a calibrated probability of truth.

Pointers to stored statements used by the procedure that proposed the prediction.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

These pointers allow cascade retraction: removing an entity removes its own statements, then generated statements that cite those statements, then further generated statements that cite those outputs. The traversal follows only the designated provenance links; it does not delete curated neighbours merely because they are connected through ordinary graph relationships.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

The crucial distinction

The paper calls its dependency record “selection provenance.” It records why the procedure proposed a missing subject–predicate slot—not evidence supporting the predicted object. The model itself predicts the object from the subject and predicate labels alone; it does not receive the cited statements as input.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Consequently, Loka can answer “Which stored predictions must be withdrawn under this dependency policy?” It cannot establish “Which sources prove this prediction is correct?” Nor does retraction remove a source’s influence from the model’s training.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Main results
Evaluation Reported result
Synthetic correctness Matched an independent reference on all 700 tested roots after finding and fixing an annotation-cleanup defect.
Large synthetic retraction Computed a 106,255-row removal set from a roughly 5-million-row store in about 85 ms in memory; persistent deletion was measured separately.
Real-data correctness On a roughly 2-million-triple Wikidata store, matched all 8,621 required removals, counted as entity–generated-triple pairs.
Dedicated traversal versus queries Computed equivalent retraction sets 6–10× faster than SPARQL-star queries through Loka’s own general query executor.
Prediction quality The transformer scored below a predicate-frequency baseline: MRR 0.115 versus 0.129 on 19,686 rankable held-out queries.

These are results reported by the paper, not an independent replication.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Important limits

Retraction is entity-level, not arbitrary single-statement deletion. The record cites only one statement per contributing neighbour, which suffices for removing the whole neighbour but can miss dependencies under statement-level deletion.

Alternative derivations are not tracked separately. If another writer adds the same triple with different citations, those citations merge; losing a source can remove a triple that still has another derivation.

Training-data exclusion depends on flags. Loka’s extractor excludes flagged generated statements, but another writer can insert an unflagged generated statement.

Curated annotations can remain after their underlying statement is removed. Only reserved-namespace annotations are swept automatically.

Evaluation remains bounded. Tests used one machine, real dependency chains of two generated hops, and no cross-engine retraction benchmark.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

The paper’s strongest demonstrated result is that explicitly recorded, statement-level dependency links can support predictable store-side cleanup, even when the generator is weak. Its most important qualification is that these links describe a procedural dependency policy, not factual justification or a complete account of the model’s influences.

loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Finished
2s

The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star knowledge-graph store designed to make model-generated statements identifiable, filterable, and retractable when their recorded source dependencies are removed. Its contribution is provenance infrastructure—not a better prediction model.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

What it does

Loka stores model-generated facts alongside curated facts, but adds annotations to each generated triple recording:

That it was generated.

Which model produced it.

A confidence score, which is a decoding score rather than a calibrated probability of truth.

Pointers to stored statements used by the procedure that proposed the prediction.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

These pointers allow cascade retraction: removing an entity removes its own statements, then generated statements that cite those statements, then further generated statements that cite those outputs. The traversal follows only the designated provenance links; it does not delete curated neighbours merely because they are connected through ordinary graph relationships.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

The crucial distinction

The paper calls its dependency record “selection provenance.” It records why the procedure proposed a missing subject–predicate slot—not evidence supporting the predicted object. The model itself predicts the object from the subject and predicate labels alone; it does not receive the cited statements as input.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Consequently, Loka can answer “Which stored predictions must be withdrawn under this dependency policy?” It cannot establish “Which sources prove this prediction is correct?” Nor does retraction remove a source’s influence from the model’s training.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Main results
Evaluation Reported result
Synthetic correctness Matched an independent reference on all 700 tested roots after finding and fixing an annotation-cleanup defect.
Large synthetic retraction Computed a 106,255-row removal set from a roughly 5-million-row store in about 85 ms in memory; persistent deletion was measured separately.
Real-data correctness On a roughly 2-million-triple Wikidata store, matched all 8,621 required removals, counted as entity–generated-triple pairs.
Dedicated traversal versus queries Computed equivalent retraction sets 6–10× faster than SPARQL-star queries through Loka’s own general query executor.
Prediction quality The transformer scored below a predicate-frequency baseline: MRR 0.115 versus 0.129 on 19,686 rankable held-out queries.

These are results reported by the paper, not an independent replication.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Important limits

Retraction is entity-level, not arbitrary single-statement deletion. The record cites only one statement per contributing neighbour, which suffices for removing the whole neighbour but can miss dependencies under statement-level deletion.

Alternative derivations are not tracked separately. If another writer adds the same triple with different citations, those citations merge; losing a source can remove a triple that still has another derivation.

Training-data exclusion depends on flags. Loka’s extractor excludes flagged generated statements, but another writer can insert an unflagged generated statement.

Curated annotations can remain after their underlying statement is removed. Only reserved-namespace annotations are swept automatically.

Evaluation remains bounded. Tests used one machine, real dependency chains of two generated hops, and no cross-engine retraction benchmark.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

The paper’s strongest demonstrated result is that explicitly recorded, statement-level dependency links can support predictable store-side cleanup, even when the generator is weak. Its most important qualification is that these links describe a procedural dependency policy, not factual justification or a complete account of the model’s influences.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Finished
4s
1. Summary

Loka integrates a small vocabulary for model-generated statements into an RDF-star store: generated triples receive annotations identifying their model, decoding score, and statements selected by the candidate-proposal procedure. These annotations support exclusion from exported training corpora and node-rooted cascade retraction through explicit dependency links, without traversing ordinary data edges. The paper evaluates closure correctness against an independent reference, reports in-memory and persistent-deletion timings, compares RDF-star encoding with reification and named graphs, and uses small Wikidata-trained transformers plus a frequency predictor as generators. Its most useful contribution is an implemented and tested operational policy for managing generated assertions, rather than a new provenance formalism or prediction method. The paper is commendably candid about weak model accuracy and several semantic limitations, but the relationship between recorded dependencies, actual procedural inputs, and deletion correctness needs sharper specification.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

2. Recommendation

Weak Reject for a full systems/databases research paper.

The implementation, differential testing, discovery of a real bug, and separation of closure computation from persistent deletion are positives. However, the current contribution is principally an integration of explicit dependency annotations with graph traversal, while the evaluation does not yet establish a sufficiently strong systems advantage or validate the completeness of the dependency capture. Important issues include ambiguous generation/curation identity, an unreconciled real-data row count, and a storage comparison whose named-graph baseline is explicitly nonminimal.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

This is a venue-style recommendation, not an objection to posting a preprint. For arXiv, I would revise the semantic claims and accounting before posting; the larger experimental additions could follow in a subsequent version.

3. Main weaknesses and concrete fixes
W1. The dependency contract is weaker—and less precisely defined—than the headline motivation suggests

Sections: Abstract, §§1, 3.2, 3.4, 4.4, 7.2

The paper carefully distinguishes selection provenance from evidence supporting a predicted value. That distinction is good. However, it also repeatedly describes the record as the procedure’s inputs, says the bounded selector “cites everything it used,” and calls the record complete relative to the procedure. The described selector uses more information than the listed citations obviously capture:

A neighbour’s matching statement establishes the shared (predicate, object) relationship, but the record cites one neighbour statement carrying the proposed predicate—not necessarily the matching statement.

Predicate ranking and the top-
𝑁
N cutoff can depend on competing candidates.

The “subject lacks this predicate” test is a negative condition.

Decoding and entity resolution depend on labels and a label-to-entity lookup, which are not described as dependencies.

These omissions do not necessarily invalidate the narrower whole-neighbour-deletion policy: a representative statement can serve as a deletion trigger when that neighbour is removed. But that is not equivalent to recording every consulted statement or complete procedural lineage. The paper itself acknowledges that several statements of a neighbour can matter while only one is cited.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Concrete fix: Define two separate concepts:

An execution/input record: what the procedure actually read.

A node-deletion dependency record: sufficient triggers for the explicitly supported invalidation policy.

State which one Loka implements. Give a precise completeness condition scoped to whole-node deletion, explain excluded dependencies and negative conditions, and replace “cites everything it used” unless that stronger claim is demonstrated.

W2. Correctness testing validates traversal, not dependency capture

Sections: §§6.1–6.2, 6.5

The synthetic reference independently computes closure over generated dependency lists, and the real-data reference computes closure from recorded citations. These are valuable tests of retract_set, including annotation cleanup. They do not independently establish that the selector wrote every edge required by the intended policy. A missing citation could be absent from both the store and the reference closure, producing perfect agreement. Replacing the transformer with a frequency predictor does not resolve this because selection and annotation code remain unchanged.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Concrete fix: Add a separate dependency-capture oracle. On small graphs, instrument the selector or independently enumerate contributing neighbours and required node-deletion triggers, then compare that result with emitted annotations. Include cases with multiple matches per neighbour, bounds, ties, normalization, and generated context. Deliberately remove a required citation to show that this test fails even when closure-agreement tests still pass.

W3. Assertion identity is conflated with generation identity

Sections: §§2.5, 3.1–3.4, 7.2

Annotations attach to the content of a triple, rather than to a particular assertion or generation event. The paper acknowledges merged citations from multiple generated derivations and consequent over-deletion. The more consequential unresolved case is a triple that is both generated and independently curated: the representation does not explain how curated ownership survives a generated flag or cascade deletion. The supplied pipeline avoids some duplicates, but the store explicitly accepts other writers.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Restrict the supported model to a single-writer, disjoint curated/generated assertion space and enforce that restriction; or

Introduce assertion/generation-event identifiers, separate curated support from generated support, and delete the asserted triple only when the chosen support policy permits it.

Add tests for generated→curated promotion, curated/generated collisions, two generating models, and withdrawal of only one support.

Sections: §§1–2, 3.4

The paper appropriately acknowledges truth maintenance and deletion propagation, and explicitly says that propagation itself is not new. What remains is a useful integration: a reserved vocabulary, pipeline filters, a reverse quoted-triple index, and specialized traversal. The paper presents Loka, an RDF-star knowledge-graph store designed to make model-generated statements identifiable, filterable, and retractable when their recorded source dependencies are removed. Its contribution is provenance infrastructure—not a better prediction model.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

What it does

Loka stores model-generated facts alongside curated facts, but adds annotations to each generated triple recording:

That it was generated.

Which model produced it.

A confidence score, which is a decoding score rather than a calibrated probability of truth.

Pointers to stored statements used by the procedure that proposed the prediction.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

These pointers allow cascade retraction: removing an entity removes its own statements, then generated statements that cite those statements, then further generated statements that cite those outputs. The traversal follows only the designated provenance links; it does not delete curated neighbours merely because they are connected through ordinary graph relationships.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

The crucial distinction

The paper calls its dependency record “selection provenance.” It records why the procedure proposed a missing subject–predicate slot—not evidence supporting the predicted object. The model itself predicts the object from the subject and predicate labels alone; it does not receive the cited statements as input.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Consequently, Loka can answer “Which stored predictions must be withdrawn under this dependency policy?” It cannot establish “Which sources prove this prediction is correct?” Nor does retraction remove a source’s influence from the model’s training.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Main results
Evaluation Reported result
Synthetic correctness Matched an independent reference on all 700 tested roots after finding and fixing an annotation-cleanup defect.
Large synthetic retraction Computed a 106,255-row removal set from a roughly 5-million-row store in about 85 ms in memory; persistent deletion was measured separately.
Real-data correctness On a roughly 2-million-triple Wikidata store, matched all 8,621 required removals, counted as entity–generated-triple pairs.
Dedicated traversal versus queries Computed equivalent retraction sets 6–10× faster than SPARQL-star queries through Loka’s own general query executor.
Prediction quality The transformer scored below a predicate-frequency baseline: MRR 0.115 versus 0.129 on 19,686 rankable held-out queries.

These are results reported by the paper, not an independent replication.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Important limits

Retraction is entity-level, not arbitrary single-statement deletion. The record cites only one statement per contributing neighbour, which suffices for removing the whole neighbour but can miss dependencies under statement-level deletion.

Alternative derivations are not tracked separately. If another writer adds the same triple with different citations, those citations merge; losing a source can remove a triple that still has another derivation.

Training-data exclusion depends on flags. Loka’s extractor excludes flagged generated statements, but another writer can insert an unflagged generated statement.

Curated annotations can remain after their underlying statement is removed. Only reserved-namespace annotations are swept automatically.

Evaluation remains bounded. Tests used one machine, real dependency chains of two generated hops, and no cross-engine retraction benchmark.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

The paper’s strongest demonstrated result is that explicitly recorded, statement-level dependency links can support predictable store-side cleanup, even when the generator is weak. Its most important qualification is that these links describe a procedural dependency policy, not factual justification or a complete account of the model’s influences.

1. Summary

Loka integrates a small vocabulary for model-generated statements into an RDF-star store: generated triples receive annotations identifying their model, decoding score, and statements selected by the candidate-proposal procedure. These annotations support exclusion from exported training corpora and node-rooted cascade retraction through explicit dependency links, without traversing ordinary data edges. The paper evaluates closure correctness against an independent reference, reports in-memory and persistent-deletion timings, compares RDF-star encoding with reification and named graphs, and uses small Wikidata-trained transformers plus a frequency predictor as generators. Its most useful contribution is an implemented and tested operational policy for managing generated assertions, rather than a new provenance formalism or prediction method. The paper is commendably candid about weak model accuracy and several semantic limitations, but the relationship between recorded dependencies, actual procedural inputs, and deletion correctness needs sharper specification.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

2. Recommendation

Weak Reject for a full systems/databases research paper.

The implementation, differential testing, discovery of a real bug, and separation of closure computation from persistent deletion are positives. However, the current contribution is principally an integration of explicit dependency annotations with graph traversal, while the evaluation does not yet establish a sufficiently strong systems advantage or validate the completeness of the dependency capture. Important issues include ambiguous generation/curation identity, an unreconciled real-data row count, and a storage comparison whose named-graph baseline is explicitly nonminimal.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

This is a venue-style recommendation, not an objection to posting a preprint. For arXiv, I would revise the semantic claims and accounting before posting; the larger experimental additions could follow in a subsequent version.

3. Main weaknesses and concrete fixes
W1. The dependency contract is weaker—and less precisely defined—than the headline motivation suggests

Sections: Abstract, §§1, 3.2, 3.4, 4.4, 7.2

The paper carefully distinguishes selection provenance from evidence supporting a predicted value. That distinction is good. However, it also repeatedly describes the record as the procedure’s inputs, says the bounded selector “cites everything it used,” and calls the record complete relative to the procedure. The described selector uses more information than the listed citations obviously capture:

A neighbour’s matching statement establishes the shared (predicate, object) relationship, but the record cites one neighbour statement carrying the proposed predicate—not necessarily the matching statement.

Predicate ranking and the top-
𝑁
N cutoff can depend on competing candidates.

The “subject lacks this predicate” test is a negative condition.

Decoding and entity resolution depend on labels and a label-to-entity lookup, which are not described as dependencies.

These omissions do not necessarily invalidate the narrower whole-neighbour-deletion policy: a representative statement can serve as a deletion trigger when that neighbour is removed. But that is not equivalent to recording every consulted statement or complete procedural lineage. The paper itself acknowledges that several statements of a neighbour can matter while only one is cited.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Concrete fix: Define two separate concepts:

An execution/input record: what the procedure actually read.

A node-deletion dependency record: sufficient triggers for the explicitly supported invalidation policy.

State which one Loka implements. Give a precise completeness condition scoped to whole-node deletion, explain excluded dependencies and negative conditions, and replace “cites everything it used” unless that stronger claim is demonstrated.

W2. Correctness testing validates traversal, not dependency capture

Sections: §§6.1–6.2, 6.5

The synthetic reference independently computes closure over generated dependency lists, and the real-data reference computes closure from recorded citations. These are valuable tests of retract_set, including annotation cleanup. They do not independently establish that the selector wrote every edge required by the intended policy. A missing citation could be absent from both the store and the reference closure, producing perfect agreement. Replacing the transformer with a frequency predictor does not resolve this because selection and annotation code remain unchanged.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Concrete fix: Add a separate dependency-capture oracle. On small graphs, instrument the selector or independently enumerate contributing neighbours and required node-deletion triggers, then compare that result with emitted annotations. Include cases with multiple matches per neighbour, bounds, ties, normalization, and generated context. Deliberately remove a required citation to show that this test fails even when closure-agreement tests still pass.

W3. Assertion identity is conflated with generation identity

Sections: §§2.5, 3.1–3.4, 7.2

Annotations attach to the content of a triple, rather than to a particular assertion or generation event. The paper acknowledges merged citations from multiple generated derivations and consequent over-deletion. The more consequential unresolved case is a triple that is both generated and independently curated: the representation does not explain how curated ownership survives a generated flag or cascade deletion. The supplied pipeline avoids some duplicates, but the store explicitly accepts other writers.
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf

Concrete fix: Either:

Restrict the supported model to a single-writer, disjoint curated/generated assertion space and enforce that restriction; or

Introduce assertion/generation-event identifiers, separate curated support from generated support, and delete the asserted triple only when the chosen support policy permits it.

Add tests for generated→curated promotion, curated/generated collisions, two generating models, and withdrawal of only one support.

W4. Novelty is insufficiently isolated from the engineering integration

Sections: §§1–2, 3.4

The paper appropriately acknowledges truth maintenance and deletion propagation, and explicitly says that propagation itself is not new. What remains is a useful integration: a reserved vocabulary, pipeline filters, a reverse quoted-triple index, and specialized traversal. Title: Loka paper review - DeepSeek
URL: https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/a8080cd7-2910-4e0a-97b7-605db1320b40
Source element: <body>
---
New chat
Today
Loka paper review
30 Days
Academy Maniacs
Emma Leonhart
Loka paper review
loka-retractable-provenance.pdf
PDF 165.6KB
/databases venue. Review the attached paper, which is about to be submitted to arXiv (cs.DB). Give: (1) a one-paragraph summary; (2) a recommendation (Strong Accept / Accept / Weak Accept / Weak Reject / Reject); (3) the main weaknesses, each with the section it concerns and a concrete fix; (4) any claims that are overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent with the paper's own tables; (5) minor issues (clarity, terminology, citations). Be specific and cite section numbers.
(1) Summary

Loka is a system paper about keeping model-generated triples inside an RDF-star triplestore while preserving enough provenance to (a) exclude generated statements from corpora extracted from the store and (b) retract generated statements by dependency when a curated source statement is withdrawn. The authors define a small reserved-namespace annotation vocabulary (propositionGenerated, propositionGeneratedBy, propositionConfidence, propositionSelectedFrom, propositionPredictedLabel) attached to each generated triple as RDF-star annotations. propositionSelectedFrom records "selection provenance": the stored statements the candidate-selection procedure consulted when proposing a (subject, predicate) slot—explicitly not a justification of the predicted object. Retraction (retract_set, §3.4) takes a root node, removes its rows, then follows only propositionSelectedFrom edges within the reserved namespace to a fixpoint, sweeping annotation rows of removed generated triples. The system is evaluated against an independent reference implementation on synthetic graphs (agreement on 700 roots after fixing one defect, §6.1), timed (≈85 ms for a 106k-triple removal set in a 5M-row in-memory store, §6.2), compared against a plain SPARQL-star closure (6–10× faster, §6.2), compared against reification/PROV-O and named-graph encodings by row and byte count (§6.3), and checked on real Wikidata stores of 153k and 2M triples with two-hop generated dependency chains (§6.2). A case-study series of small from-scratch masked-triple transformers (v3–v14) supplies the workload; the authors are candid that the model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline on held-out triples (§6.4).

(2) Recommendation

Weak Accept. The core contribution—a fixed RDF-star annotation block with an operational semantics for cascade retraction bounded to a reserved namespace—is modest but real, cleanly specified, and empirically checked against an independent reference and on real data. The engineering and reproducibility are unusually thorough. However, the paper is long for its contribution, the evaluation is single-machine with two data points isolating store size, the real-data chain depth is only two generated hops, and several framing claims outrun the evidence. It is a reasonable cs.DB systems contribution, but it needs tightening and a few claims corrected before it reads as more than a careful engineering report.

(3) Main weaknesses

W1. The contribution is narrower than the framing suggests; related-work positioning is thin on the store side (§1, §2.2, §2.5). The paper says "what we add is not a provenance vocabulary but an operational use of it inside the store" (§2.2), which is honest, but the comparison to TripleProv (Wylot et al., 2014), which also stores provenance in a native RDF store and answers lineage natively, is one sentence. The specific delta—RDF-star statement-level annotation vs. named graphs/reification, and reserved-namespace-bounded traversal—is asserted rather than demonstrated against TripleProv. Fix: add a short comparison table (granularity, storage cost, query interface, retraction support) covering TripleProv, named graphs, nanopublications, and Loka, and cite what TripleProv's deletion/lineage behavior actually is. Also state explicitly in §1 that the retraction algorithm itself is standard fixpoint propagation (as §2.5 admits) so the novelty claim is only the realization plus the namespace bounding.

W2. Evaluation is single-machine and the store-size isolation rests on two data points (§6.2, §7.3). The paper itself concedes this ("the comparison that isolates store size is therefore the pair of large rows, which is two data points"; "on one machine"). The claim that cost follows removal size rather than store size is thus weakly supported, and the per-triple cost varies 0.31–0.8 µs across rows with an unexplained factor (depth vs. size). Fix: either add a third large store size (e.g., 2M and 20M rows with equal removal sets) or soften the claim in the abstract and conclusion to "consistent with" and move the two-point limitation into the abstract. Also report the depth-controlled experiment the paper says it did not isolate (fix removal-set size, vary depth).

W3. Real-data retraction chains are shallow (two generated hops) and the synthetic generator uses a reduced schema (§6.1–6.2, §7.3). The synthetic correctness test omits the generated flag, confidence, and predicted-label rows, justified by "the engine follows only propositionSelectedFrom and sweeps every annotation under the reserved prefix alike." That is plausible but not tested with the full production schema on synthetic graphs; only the 153k/2M real stores use the full schema, and there only two generated hops were built. Fix: run the 50 small / 10 medium synthetic graphs with the full production annotation block (cheap), and build at least a three-hop real chain on the 153k store to confirm termination and closure agreement at depth ≥3.

W4. "Selection provenance" is only complete relative to a bounded selector; the completeness claim needs sharper statement (§4.4, §7.2). The bounded selector consults at most 20 subject statements and 20 neighbours; citations beyond that are not consulted and therefore not recorded. The paper states this in §7.2 ("Provenance is complete relative to what the bounded selector consulted") but the abstract and §1 say the record covers "the stored statements the prediction procedure took as input" without the bound. A reader could take that as full input provenance. Fix: qualify the abstract/§1 claim with "within the selector's bounds," and report how often the bound binds on the real stores (the observed maxima 26–39 suggest it rarely does, but say so).

W5. Overstated or under-supported claims (see also §4). Several specific statements are stronger than the tables support:

Abstract: "computes the set for a 106k-triple removal from a 5M-row store in about 85 ms in memory" — fine, but the abstract omits that this is the median of five runs on one laptop and that §6.2 reports 82.0–104.6 ms range; "about 85 ms" is defensible but should carry "median."

§6.2: "These results are consistent with time following the size of the removed set rather than the size of the store, as the algorithm's per-triple index lookups predict, but they do not establish it in general" — this is appropriately hedged here, but the Conclusion (§9) drops the hedge: "with cost that, on the two large synthetic data points that isolate store size, follows the size of the removal rather than of the store." That is a two-point inference stated as a finding. Fix: align §9 with §6.2's hedge.

§3.4 and §6.1: "The comparison found a defect on its first run" is presented as a strength (good practice), but the defect (depth-0 annotation rows not swept) means the released v0.4.7 fix is what was tested; the paper should state whether any results in §6.2/§6.3 were run before or after the fix. The release notes mention "the retraction fix of §6.1" in Software and data, so presumably after—say so explicitly in §6.1.

§4.4 / §6.2: "a median of 17 citations each, maximum 39" and earlier "maximum 26 for the v13 model and 36 for the predicate-frequency generator on the 153k-triple graph" — the §6.2 text says "a median of 17 citations each, maximum 39" for the 2M store, consistent. But the §6.5 table reports "9 / 10.5 / 20 / 26" for v13 on 153k and "9 / 10.5 / 19 / 36" for the frequency generator — the p90/max differ but medians/means match, which the text says. Fine; just ensure the §6.2 "17" is clearly the 2M-store figure, since the adjacent 153k figures are 9.

W6. Link-prediction evaluation is too weak to support even the modest "workload" role (§6.4, §7.1, §7.3). The paper is upfront ("Neither learned model beats predicate frequency on this split"), and says the model is "the workload, not a contribution." That is acceptable, but the evaluation then spends a full subsection and a table on it. Fix: either move §6.4 to an appendix, or reduce it to one paragraph; the space is better spent on W2/W3. If kept, state the held-out set size (19,686) and skew explicitly in the table caption, not just the text.

W7. The reserved-namespace guard is only enforced in Loka's own pipeline, not the store (§3.1). The paper says this plainly ("the store accepts any triple over POST /triples"), but the abstract's "the store can query them... leave flagged statements out of the corpora it extracts, and retract" could be read as a store-level guarantee. Fix: add one sentence to the abstract noting that exclusion/retraction assume writers use the pipeline or set the flag; a generated triple written without the flag is not excluded. This is an important scoping caveat for a databases audience.

(4) Claims that are overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent with the paper's own tables

Abstract, "about 85 ms": §6.2 table gives 85.0 ms median (80.5–86.2 range) for 106,255 removed triples; §6.2 later says the two tables were measured by separate binaries and the ratio table's times are 15–20% below. "About 85 ms" is fine but is the median of one binary; say "median."

Conclusion (§9), "cost ... follows the size of the removal rather than of the store": contradicts §6.2's own hedge ("do not establish it in general"; "two data points"). Fix the conclusion.

§1, "Every model-predicted triple is written together with RDF-star annotations ... recording ... from which stored statements": true only for the §4.4 procedure; the interactive path (tools/retrieval_generate.py, §7.2) writes no propositionSelectedFrom edges, and earlier versions used "a cruder rule" (§7.2). The unqualified "every" is inconsistent with §7.2. Fix: "every triple written by the inference procedure of §4.4."

§3.4, "Because every generated triple carries propositionSelectedFrom edges...": same issue as above; the interactive generator's output is flagged but not retractable. Add "written by the §4.4 procedure."

§6.2, "on a real 2M-triple Wikidata store with chained predictions it matched an independently computed closure on all 8,621 required removals": the table in §6.2 and §6.5 report 8,621 required removals for the bounded selector with the v13 model on the 2M store? Actually §6.2 says "Over 8,621 required removals across 2,667 entities, the retraction preview matched the independent closure exclusively." The §6.5 table reports "v13 model 356 ... 127,958" and "Predicate frequency 8,637" — these are different experiments (153k graph). The abstract says "on a real 2M-triple store ... all 8,621 required removals," which matches §6.2. Consistent, but a reader cross-referencing §6.5 may be confused; add a one-line pointer in §6.5 that the 8,621 figure is the §6.2 2M store, not the 153k table.

§6.3, "RDF-star block is 2.8× smaller than reification and 2.4× smaller than named graphs; in bytes the gaps are 1.5× and 1.3×": check the table—333 vs 937 = 2.81× rows; 333 vs 785 quads = 2.36×, so "2.4×" is fine. Bytes 82,839 vs 125,570 = 1.52×; vs 106,767 = 1.29×. Consistent. But the text says "2.4× smaller than named graphs" while the named-graph variant is described as an "upper bound" because it could put cited statements in singletons "which needs fewer rows"—so the named-graph comparison is not apples-to-apples. State that the named-graph number is an upper bound in the prose, not just the table note.

§4.4, "at most 40 citations per prediction": the text says at most 20 subject statements plus one statement from each of at most 20 neighbours = 40. But "observed maxima are 26 ... 36 ... and 39 on the 2M-triple store" — 39 < 40, consistent. Fine. But the median-105 "unbounded selector" figure is on the 153k graph; say so (it does).

§6.4, "the v13 transformer's Hits@1 is 0.020 against 0.018 (about 27 more queries of 13,596 ranked first)": 0.020 vs 0.018 on 13,596 is a difference of ~27 queries, consistent; but the text says "the v13 transformer ranks above the untuned TransE, but with no tuning ... we do not read that as a comparison of methods." Good hedging; leave it.

§7.2, "Earlier outputs used a cruder rule ... should be re-generated before relying on retraction": this means some released stores/checkpoints may be incompatible with the retraction guarantee. Since checkpoints and corpora are released and the paper claims reproducibility, state which released artifacts (if any) were produced under the old rule, or confirm none of the evaluated runs were.

(5) Minor issues

Terminology: propositionSelectedFrom was renamed from propositionInferredFrom; §3.1 notes the engine "still follows the old IRI" for the real-data stores. This is a landmine for replicators: the released v0.4.7 code follows the old IRI, but the paper's schema table shows the new name. Add a one-line note in §3.2 or the Software section specifying which IRI the v0.4.7 release emits and follows, and whether a migration exists.

§2.1 example: the RDF-star example uses <:<Tokyo :population "13929286"> with a stray <:; the notation elsewhere is <<...>>. Fix the typo.

§3.1 table: propositionImportedFrom is listed as "Reserved; not currently emitted in production (was found redundant...)"—if it is reserved but unused, say whether the prefix-matching guards still reserve it (they match the prefix, so yes), and whether it appears in any released store.

§4.2, "Drop rows with non-IRI predicates": says "RDF does not allow a literal in the predicate position"—strictly, RDF 1.1 predicates are IRIs (and RDF-star quoted triples can have triple terms in subject/object, not predicate); the phrasing is fine but say "RDF 1.1 predicates must be IRIs."

§4.3 table: v3 row says "256 8 4 16,012,800 5 53.43" but §5.2 says stripping datatypes "raised perplexity (92.5 vs 53.4)" for v3 vs v4—check that the table's 53.43 is v3 pre-cleanup and 92.48 is v4, consistent with Appendix A (v3 53.43, v4 92.48). Fine, but the §4.3 table only shows v3; the "v3's low perplexity comes from memorising datatype-suffix tokens" sentence appears in §4.3 before §5.2 explains it—move or forward-reference.

§5.5: "a 50 M-triple extraction impractical"—the evaluated stores are 153k and 2M; say what the 50M figure refers to (the full streamed corpus?), since it is otherwise unmotivated.

§6.2, "the importer rejected 2,139 lines, 1.4%, and since the pulled file was not kept their cause can no longer be determined": this is a reproducibility gap. If possible, re-pull and diagnose; otherwise flag it in §7.3.

§6.4 table: "Predicate frequency all 19,686 0.129 0.090 0.131 0.202" vs v13 "0.115 0.085 0.118 0.170" — bold on the frequency row; fine. But the "entity-valued" row for frequency is 6,090 and literal-valued 13,596, summing to 19,686; state that in the caption.

§7.2, "Curated annotations outlive their triple": pinned by a unit test, good; but the paper should say whether the released store after a retraction is queryable without error (it is, per the text) and whether re-asserting the quoted triple later would "revive" orphan annotations—an interesting semantic question worth one sentence.

Citations: PROV-O is cited (Lebo et al., 2013) and §2.2 mentions prov:used vs prov:wasDerivedFrom; a short example mapping propositionSelectedFrom to prov:used would strengthen §2.2. Hartig 2017 is cited for RDF-star foundations; also cite the W3C RDF-star CG report in §2.1 (it appears only in References). Gupta et al. 1993 is cited for deletion propagation; the paper correctly notes the one-justification simplification—good.

§3.1 query: the SPARQL-star FILTER uses ?_g but the SELECT projects only ?s ?p ?o; the filter is fine, but add a comment that FILTER NOT EXISTS on the annotation block is the only generated-flag filter and that annotation rows are dropped by the prefix filter (the text says this; the query alone doesn't show the prefix filter—show both or say "plus a prefix filter not shown").

Abstract, "small transformers trained from scratch on Wikidata": §7.3 notes entities are identified by English label so same-label entities merge; this affects the workload, and the abstract should not imply Wikidata-scale fidelity. One clause suffices.

Formatting: the paper is ~17 pages with a 16-row reference list and dense tables; for arXiv cs.DB, consider moving §6.3 (encoding comparison) and §6.4 (link prediction) to an appendix to bring the main body to ~12 pages, which would sharpen the systems contribution.

Bottom line: the provenance vocabulary and the retraction semantics are sound and the evaluation is honest about the model's weakness, but the paper should (i) soften the two-point store-size claim in the abstract/conclusion, (ii) qualify "every generated triple" by the §4.4 procedure and the selector bounds, (iii) add a real TripleProv/named-graph comparison, and (iv) run the synthetic correctness test with the full production annotation block. With those changes I would move to Accept.

A case-study series of small from-scratch masked-triple transformers (v3–v14) supplies the workload; the authors are candid that the model does not beat a predicate-frequency baseline on held-out triples (§6.4).

(2) Recommendation

Weak Accept. The core contribution—a fixed RDF-star annotation block with an operational semantics for cascade retraction bounded to a reserved namespace—is modest but real, cleanly specified, and empirically checked against an independent reference and on real data. The engineering and reproducibility are unusually thorough. However, the paper is long for its contribution, the evaluation is single-machine with two data points isolating store size, the real-data chain depth is only two generated hops, and several framing claims outrun the evidence. It is a reasonable cs.DB systems contribution, but it needs tightening and a few claims corrected before it reads as more than a careful engineering report.

(3) Main weaknesses

W1. The contribution is narrower than the framing suggests; related-work positioning is thin on the store side (§1, §2.2, §2.5). The paper says "what we add is not a provenance vocabulary but an operational use of it inside the store" (§2.2), which is honest, but the comparison to TripleProv (Wylot et al., 2014), which also stores provenance in a native RDF store and answers lineage natively, is one sentence. The specific delta—RDF-star statement-level annotation vs. named graphs/reification, and reserved-namespace-bounded traversal—is asserted rather than demonstrated against TripleProv. Fix: add a short comparison table (granularity, storage cost, query interface, retraction support) covering TripleProv, named graphs, nanopublications, and Loka, and cite what TripleProv's deletion/lineage behavior actually is. Also state explicitly in §1 that the retraction algorithm itself is standard fixpoint propagation (as §2.5 admits) so the novelty claim is only the realization plus the namespace bounding.

W2. Evaluation is single-machine and the store-size isolation rests on two data points (§6.2, §7.3). The paper itself concedes this ("the comparison that isolates store size is therefore the pair of large rows, which is two data points"; "on one machine"). The claim that cost follows removal size rather than store size is thus weakly supported, and the per-triple cost varies 0.31–0.8 µs across rows with an unexplained factor (depth vs. size). Fix: either add a third large store size (e.g., 2M and 20M rows with equal removal sets) or soften the claim in the abstract and conclusion to "consistent with" and move the two-point limitation into the abstract. Also report the depth-controlled experiment the paper says it did not isolate (fix removal-set size, vary depth).

W3. Real-data retraction chains are shallow (two generated hops) and the synthetic generator uses a reduced schema (§6.1–6.2, §7.3). The synthetic correctness test omits the generated flag, confidence, and predicted-label rows, justified by "the engine follows only propositionSelectedFrom and sweeps every annotation under the reserved prefix alike." That is plausible but not tested with the full production schema on synthetic graphs; only the 153k/2M real stores use the full schema, and there only two generated hops were built. Fix: run the 50 small / 10 medium synthetic graphs with the full production annotation block (cheap), and build at least a three-hop real chain on the 153k store to confirm termination and closure agreement at depth ≥3.

W4. "Selection provenance" is only complete relative to a bounded selector; the completeness claim needs sharper statement (§4.4, §7.2). The bounded selector consults at most 20 subject statements and 20 neighbours; citations beyond that are not consulted and therefore not recorded. The paper states this in §7.2 ("Provenance is complete relative to what the bounded selector consulted") but the abstract and §1 say the record covers "the stored statements the prediction procedure took as input" without the bound. A reader could take that as full input provenance. Fix: qualify the abstract/§1 claim with "within the selector's bounds," and report how often the bound binds on the real stores (the observed maxima 26–39 suggest it rarely does, but say so).

W5. Overstated or under-supported claims (see also §4). Several specific statements are stronger than the tables support:

Abstract: "computes the set for a 106k-triple removal from a 5M-row store in about 85 ms in memory" — fine, but the abstract omits that this is the median of five runs on one laptop and that §6.2 reports 82.0–104.6 ms range; "about 85 ms" is defensible but should carry "median."

§6.2: "These results are consistent with time following the size of the removed set rather than the size of the store, as the algorithm's per-triple index lookups predict, but they do not establish it in general" — this is appropriately hedged here, but the Conclusion (§9) drops the hedge: "with cost that, on the two large synthetic data points that isolate store size, follows the size of the removal rather than of the store." That is a two-point inference stated as a finding. Fix: align §9 with §6.2's hedge.

§3.4 and §6.1: "The comparison found a defect on its first run" is presented as a strength (good practice), but the defect (depth-0 annotation rows not swept) means the released v0.4.7 fix is what was tested; the paper should state whether any results in §6.2/§6.3 were run before or after the fix. The release notes mention "the retraction fix of §6.1" in Software and data, so presumably after—say so explicitly in §6.1.

§4.4 / §6.2: "a median of 17 citations each, maximum 39" and earlier "maximum 26 for the v13 model and 36 for the predicate-frequency generator on the 153k-triple graph" — the §6.2 text says "a median of 17 citations each, maximum 39" for the 2M store, consistent. But the §6.5 table reports "9 / 10.5 / 20 / 26" for v13 on 153k and "9 / 10.5 / 19 / 36" for the frequency generator — the p90/max differ but medians/means match, which the text says. Fine; just ensure the §6.2 "17" is clearly the 2M-store figure, since the adjacent 153k figures are 9.

W6. Link-prediction evaluation is too weak to support even the modest "workload" role (§6.4, §7.1, §7.3). The paper is upfront ("Neither learned model beats predicate frequency on this split"), and says the model is "the workload, not a contribution." That is acceptable, but the evaluation then spends a full subsection and a table on it. Fix: either move §6.4 to an appendix, or reduce it to one paragraph; the space is better spent on W2/W3. If kept, state the held-out set size (19,686) and skew explicitly in the table caption, not just the text.

W7. The reserved-namespace guard is only enforced in Loka's own pipeline, not the store (§3.1). The paper says this plainly ("the store accepts any triple over POST /triples"), but the abstract's "the store can query them... leave flagged statements out of the corpora it extracts, and retract" could be read as a store-level guarantee. Fix: add one sentence to the abstract noting that exclusion/retraction assume writers use the pipeline or set the flag; a generated triple written without the flag is not excluded. This is an important scoping caveat for a databases audience.

(4) Claims that are overstated, unsupported, or inconsistent with the paper's own tables

Abstract, "about 85 ms": §6.2 table gives 85.0 ms median (80.5–86.2 range) for 106,255 removed triples; §6.2 later says the two tables were measured by separate binaries and the ratio table's times are 15–20% below. "About 85 ms" is fine but is the median of one binary; say "median."

Conclusion (§9), "cost ... follows the size of the removal rather than of the store": contradicts §6.2's own hedge ("do not establish it in general"; "two data points"). Fix the conclusion.

§1, "Every model-predicted triple is written together with RDF-star annotations ... recording ... from which stored statements": true only for the §4.4 procedure; the interactive path (tools/retrieval_generate.py, §7.2) writes no propositionSelectedFrom edges, and earlier versions used "a cruder rule" (§7.2). The unqualified "every" is inconsistent with §7.2. Fix: "every triple written by the inference procedure of §4.4."

§3.4, "Because every generated triple carries propositionSelectedFrom edges...": same issue as above; the interactive generator's output is flagged but not retractable. Add "written by the §4.4 procedure."

§6.2, "on a real 2M-triple Wikidata store with chained predictions it matched an independently computed closure on all 8,621 required removals": the table in §6.2 and §6.5 report 8,621 required removals for the bounded selector with the v13 model on the 2M store? Actually §6.2 says "Over 8,621 required removals across 2,667 entities, the retraction preview matched the independent closure exclusively." The §6.5 table reports "v13 model 356 ... 127,958" and "Predicate frequency 8,637" — these are different experiments (153k graph). The abstract says "on a real 2M-triple store ... all 8,621 required removals," which matches §6.2. Consistent, but a reader cross-referencing §6.5 may be confused; add a one-line pointer in §6.5 that the 8,621 figure is the §6.2 2M store, not the 153k table.

§6.3, "RDF-star block is 2.8× smaller than reification and 2.4× smaller than named graphs; in bytes the gaps are 1.5× and 1.3×": check the table—333 vs 937 = 2.81× rows; 333 vs 785 quads = 2.36×, so "2.4×" is fine. Bytes 82,839 vs 125,570 = 1.52×; vs 106,767 = 1.29×. Consistent. But the text says "2.4× smaller than named graphs" while the named-graph variant is described as an "upper bound" because it could put cited statements in singletons "which needs fewer rows"—so the named-graph comparison is not apples-to-apples. State that the named-graph number is an upper bound in the prose, not just the table note.

§4.4, "at most 40 citations per prediction": the text says at most 20 subject statements plus one statement from each of at most 20 neighbours = 40. But "observed maxima are 26 ... 36 ... and 39 on the 2M-triple store" — 39 < 40, consistent. Fine. But the median-105 "unbounded selector" figure is on the 153k graph; say so (it does).

§6.4, "the v13 transformer's Hits@1 is 0.020 against 0.018 (about 27 more queries of 13,596 ranked first)": 0.020 vs 0.018 on 13,596 is a difference of ~27 queries, consistent; but the text says "the v13 transformer ranks above the untuned TransE, but with no tuning ... we do not read that as a comparison of methods." Good hedging; leave it.

§7.2, "Earlier outputs used a cruder rule ... should be re-generated before relying on retraction": this means some released stores/checkpoints may be incompatible with the retraction guarantee. Since checkpoints and corpora are released and the paper claims reproducibility, state which released artifacts (if any) were produced under the old rule, or confirm none of the evaluated runs were.

(5) Minor issues

Terminology: propositionSelectedFrom was renamed from propositionInferredFrom; §3.1 notes the engine "still follows the old IRI" for the real-data stores. This is a landmine for replicators: the released v0.4.7 code follows the old IRI, but the paper's schema table shows the new name. Add a one-line note in §3.2 or the Software section specifying which IRI the v0.4.7 release emits and follows, and whether a migration exists.

§2.1 example: the RDF-star example uses <:<Tokyo :population "13929286"> with a stray <:; the notation elsewhere is <<...>>. Fix the typo.

§3.1 table: propositionImportedFrom is listed as "Reserved; not currently emitted in production (was found redundant...)"—if it is reserved but unused, say whether the prefix-matching guards still reserve it (they match the prefix, so yes), and whether it appears in any released store.

§4.2, "Drop rows with non-IRI predicates": says "RDF does not allow a literal in the predicate position"—strictly, RDF 1.1 predicates are IRIs (and RDF-star quoted triples can have triple terms in subject/object, not predicate); the phrasing is fine but say "RDF 1.1 predicates must be IRIs."

§4.3 table: v3 row says "256 8 4 16,012,800 5 53.43" but §5.2 says stripping datatypes "raised perplexity (92.5 vs 53.4)" for v3 vs v4—check that the table's 53.43 is v3 pre-cleanup and 92.48 is v4, consistent with Appendix A (v3 53.43, v4 92.48). Fine, but the §4.3 table only shows v3; the "v3's low perplexity comes from memorising datatype-suffix tokens" sentence appears in §4.3 before §5.2 explains it—move or forward-reference.

§5.5: "a 50 M-triple extraction impractical"—the evaluated stores are 153k and 2M; say what the 50M figure refers to (the full streamed corpus?), since it is otherwise unmotivated.

§6.2, "the importer rejected 2,139 lines, 1.4%, and since the pulled file was not kept their cause can no longer be determined": this is a reproducibility gap. If possible, re-pull and diagnose; otherwise flag it in §7.3.

§6.4 table: "Predicate frequency all 19,686 0.129 0.090 0.131 0.202" vs v13 "0.115 0.085 0.118 0.170" — bold on the frequency row; fine. But the "entity-valued" row for frequency is 6,090 and literal-valued 13,596, summing to 19,686; state that in the caption.

§7.2, "Curated annotations outlive their triple": pinned by a unit test, good; but the paper should say whether the released store after a retraction is queryable without error (it is, per the text) and whether re-asserting the quoted triple later would "revive" orphan annotations—an interesting semantic question worth one sentence.

Citations: PROV-O is cited (Lebo et al., 2013) and §2.2 mentions prov:used vs prov:wasDerivedFrom; a short example mapping propositionSelectedFrom to prov:used would strengthen §2.2. Hartig 2017 is cited for RDF-star foundations; also cite the W3C RDF-star CG report in §2.1 (it appears only in References). Gupta et al. 1993 is cited for deletion propagation; the paper correctly notes the one-justification simplification—good.

§3.1 query: the SPARQL-star FILTER uses ?_g but the SELECT projects only ?s ?p ?o; the filter is fine, but add a comment that FILTER NOT EXISTS on the annotation block is the only generated-flag filter and that annotation rows are dropped by the prefix filter (the text says this; the query alone doesn't show the prefix filter—show both or say "plus a prefix filter not shown").

Abstract, "small transformers trained from scratch on Wikidata": §7.3 notes entities are identified by English label so same-label entities merge; this affects the workload, and the abstract should not imply Wikidata-scale fidelity. One clause suffices.

Formatting: the paper is ~17 pages with a 16-row reference list and dense tables; for arXiv cs.DB, consider moving §6.3 (encoding comparison) and §6.4 (link prediction) to an appendix to bring the main body to ~12 pages, which would sharpen the systems contribution.

Bottom line: the provenance vocabulary and the retraction semantics are sound and the evaluation is honest about the model's weakness, but the paper should (i) soften the two-point store-size claim in the abstract/conclusion, (ii) qualify "every generated triple" by the §4.4 procedure and the selector bounds, (iii) add a real TripleProv/named-graph comparison, and (iv) run the synthetic correctness test with the full production annotation block. With those changes I would move to Accept.
